sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Evaluate whether early outpatient metformin, ivermectin or fluvoxamine reduces later provider-diagnosed long COVID. Long COVID was added during recruitment in April 2021; the corrected appendix traces its initial primary-outcome listing, later secondary status, and pre-unblinding analysis-plan timing. The relevant claim is prevention of a later diagnosis after acute-infection treatment, not treatment of established long COVID. The evolving endpoint must be described rather than presented as an unchanged original primary outcome. COVID-OUT supplies a randomized prevention signal in a selected acute-infection population. Benefit for current recurrent-infection populations, symptom-defined long COVID and established illness is not established by this report. Independent contemporary trials with complete follow-up, clear endpoint definitions and prespecified analyses could strengthen or weaken the prevention conclusion. Do not infer an individual treatment decision from this study alone.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Human adults aged 30-85 with overweight or obesity and a recent SARS-CoV-2 infection. Six US sites recruited remotely; symptoms under 7 days, positive test within 3 days, no known previous infection. Pregnancy was permitted for metformin randomization. 1431 randomized; 1323 in the acute modified intention-to-treat population; 1126 entered this long-term analysis, including 564 assigned metformin and 562 matched placebo. The 1126 participants are a selected follow-up population, not all randomized participants. Oral metformin tablets; the related acute report identifies immediate release, not an extended-release comparison. The studied course used 500 mg on day 1, 500 mg twice daily on days 2-5, then 500 mg morning and 1000 mg evening through day 14. A factorial design included ivermectin, fluvoxamine or their matched placebos; other treatments after enrollment were recorded. Acute follow-up was 28 days; long-term surveys continued to day 300. These are study exposures, not a recommended self-treatment schedule. Identical metformin placebo, with concurrently randomized controls. Equal allocation to available arms, stratified by site; women pregnant or lactating entered only the metformin/placebo comparison. A pregenerated mass-weighted urn sequence was implemented through a password-protected application; allocation was concealed except from the responsible statistician and pharmacists. Participants, investigators, treating clinicians and outcome assessors were masked; matched pills, opaque packaging and coded packets supported concealment. Recruitment ran December 2020 to January 2022; the factorial arms opened and closed at different dates. Balanced factorial assignments support the metformin contrast; reports of different outcomes remain one trial family. 28/564 metformin and 24/562 placebo participants were lost before day 270. 1074/1126 completed at least 9 months or reported a diagnosis; those without a diagnosis were censored at their final completed survey. At least one received dose was required for the original modified intention-to-treat analysis; exact complete-course adherence is not quantified in this long-term report. People never receiving a dose and people not entering qualifying long-term follow-up were excluded from this analysis. Modified intention-to-treat followed by a consenting long-term analysis cohort; it is not a full randomized-population estimand. The individual participant is the unit; repeated surveys and factorial comparisons do not increase independent sample size. Censoring and selection can bias estimates if related to unobserved long COVID risk. Similar measured attrition does not prove missingness was noninformative.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Long COVID diagnosis was a prespecified secondary outcome by the final pre-unblinding protocol; acute severe COVID was the primary outcome. Participants reported whether a medical provider had diagnosed long COVID and the approximate date; medical records were requested. Diagnoses were assessed through 300 days, with diagnosis questions in surveys from day 180 onward. A clinical diagnosis outcome, not direct enumeration of every persistent symptom or a biological cure. No continuous symptom-scale minimal important difference applies to the binary diagnosis endpoint. Diagnosis depends partly on access to care and recognition; it is not interchangeable with symptom-based long COVID definitions. Table S4 reports day-300 cumulative incidence 6.3% (95% CI 4.2-8.2) for metformin and 10.4% (7.8-12.9) for placebo. Observed diagnoses were 35/564 for metformin and 58/562 for placebo; the observed proportions 6.2% and 10.3% differ from the Kaplan-Meier estimates. The reported absolute reduction is 4.1 percentage points (95% CI 0.9-7.4); unadjusted HR 0.587 (0.386-0.893), rounded in the main Results to 0.59 (0.39-0.89). Between randomized treatment assignments; the adjusted HR is 0.599 (0.393-0.911), not a second independent result. The confidence interval excludes an HR of 1 for this endpoint, but does not establish the same benefit for every subgroup. Use the concordant current Results and corrected Table S4. The Discussion retains a discordant 10.6% placebo value; do not silently erase it or calculate from it. C-PREVENT-CO: fewer later provider diagnoses after early acute treatment in this trial. Supports a bounded prevention signal; does not support treatment of existing long COVID, universal prevention, or equivalence of formulations. Observed estimates are distinct from the authors' implementation advocacy; the editorial interpretation retains endpoint, cohort and applicability limits. The guide can cite the corrected-table estimates with an explicit note about the residual Discussion inconsistency.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Long-term report refers safety ascertainment to the acute companion publication. The 1126 long-term respondents are not automatically the correct denominator for every acute adverse-event analysis. The current registry lists non-COVID adverse events through day 14 and serious events through day 28, with nonsystematic ascertainment for listed nonserious events. It records zero participants with serious drug-related adverse events in all six allocation arms and one all-cause death in the metformin-plus-ivermectin arm; this must not be interpreted as zero treatment risk. Current NCT04510194 results report 14-day all-cause drug discontinuation by six allocation arms: metformin only 56/284, double placebo 49/295, ivermectin only 25/206, fluvoxamine only 32/159, metformin plus fluvoxamine 50/175, and metformin plus ivermectin 29/204. These are allocation-arm counts, not three independent comparisons or all drug-attributable harms. The drug exposure lasted 14 days, whereas diagnosis follow-up extended to 300 days. This prevention report cannot establish comprehensive or long-term drug safety; it also cannot override prescribing-label contraindications. Masking and concealed allocation reduce some biases; selective entry into long-term follow-up and provider-diagnosis ascertainment remain important concerns. Randomization reduces baseline confounding; adjusted models included other trial drugs and vaccination status. Outcome status changed during the trial, as documented in Table S8; original protocol/SAP versions have not all been directly re-read here. Subgroup estimates are low-powered and numerous; an earlier-start subgroup is not proof that timing modifies treatment effect. Only 93 total diagnoses occurred; subgroup estimates are especially imprecise. Current Discussion says 10.6% placebo incidence, versus Results and corrected Table S4 10.4%. The current registry also lists 59 placebo diagnoses versus 58 in corrected Table S4, with 35 metformin diagnoses in both. The guide uses the identified corrected report estimates and retains these source discrepancies; it does not silently reconcile participant-level differences. A positive secondary outcome is informative but should not be turned into universal prevention advice. Most directly relevant to early outpatient treatment in adults with overweight/obesity and no known previous infection. The studied immediate-release course does not establish equivalence to extended release or a different duration. Prevention of a provider diagnosis differs from treating fatigue or other symptoms in established illness. Younger adults, normal-BMI adults, recurrent infection, current variants and heavily boosted populations were not all represented adequately. Present the result next to the later prevention and established-illness trials, with their different populations and endpoints.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: S-COVIDOUT-2023 / NCT04510194. COND-C02-COVIDOUT-2022 reports acute outcomes and MF-COVID-VIRAL-2024 reports viral load from the same trial. These overlapping reports must not be counted as three independent clinical trials. This reconciliation covers the current guide inventory and retrieved publisher records, not an exhaustive new systematic search. The viral-load companion may support mechanism; it cannot independently replicate the clinical prevention outcome. Carolyn T. Bramante and colleagues, including the COVID-OUT Study Team added by correction. Investigator-initiated multicenter US decentralized trial. Parsemus Foundation, Rainwater Charitable Foundation, Fast Grants and UnitedHealth Group Foundation; investigators also disclose institutional/NIH support. Funders reportedly had no design, data or writing role. Apotex supplied fluvoxamine/placebo and Edenbridge supplied ivermectin/placebo; the report does not identify these donations as metformin supply. The report lists multiple author financial relationships, including consulting, grants and holdings for J. Buse, and consulting for M. Puskarich; it does not say all authors had no conflicts. Disclosures inform scrutiny but neither prove nor disprove the randomized result. Published report with online correction effective September 1, 2023. Current publisher HTML, the correction PDF, the corrected appendix and a prior main-report PDF were obtained. Corrected appendix cover explicitly identifies September 1, 2023; Table S4 was visually inspected on PDF page 10. NCT04510194; the appendix gives the protocol/SAP change chronology, but full original version files are not all inspected in this assessment. The actual correction adds study-team authorship and corrects the appendix. It is not a retraction and does not itself specify every changed appendix cell. Publisher content was retrieved November 3, 2026 and numerical reconciliation completed November 4, 2026. Correction content and its implications are now assessed. The surviving Discussion discrepancy remains explicitly documented, not an unknown correction hold.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test early metformin against placebo for symptoms or death at day 180. The long-term primary endpoint is specified in Appendix G, distinct from the platform acute primary endpoint. Prevention after acute infection, not treatment of established long COVID. The report must be interpreted by its own endpoint hierarchy. Evidence for preventing a later clinician diagnosis is suggestive but the primary long-term symptom result was inconclusive. Magnitude, durability and applicability to current infection patterns remain uncertain. Replication with prespecified patient-important endpoints, complete follow-up and multiplicity control could strengthen or refute the signal. This is evidence for discussion, not a personal prescribing instruction.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Adults at least 30 years old; median age 47, 63% women. Ninety US sites; symptomatic infection within 7 days, positive test within 10 days; 83% reported prior vaccination or infection. 3214 randomized; 231 excluded for administrative issues or medication not delivered within 7 days; 2983 analyzed, 1439 metformin and 1544 placebo. The analysis is modified intention to treat, not all randomized participants. Aurobindo immediate-release metformin 500-mg tablets. Oral 500 mg day 1, 500 mg twice daily days 2–5, then 500 mg morning and 1000 mg evening through day 14. Usual clinical care; no simultaneous enrollment in other active platform drug comparisons. Long-term surveys at days 90, 120 and 180. This short acute regimen cannot establish the effects of chronic treatment. Placebo; 134 placebo recipients received generic placebo before the matching product became available. Parallel 1:1 allocation. Simple random-number sequence. Double-blind design, with a reported early placebo-matching limitation. Concurrent enrollment September 2023 to May 2024. Differences in medication delivery and placebo appearance are relevant implementation limitations. 300 metformin and 293 placebo participants lacked day-180 primary data. Bayesian Markov model used observed longitudinal data with adjustment; missing-at-random assumptions remain consequential. Full adherence distribution is not provided in this long-term report. Administrative and late-delivery exclusions occurred after randomization; recent reinfection within 28 days was excluded for the long-term endpoint. Modified intention-to-treat, 2983 medication recipients. Individual participant, not each repeated survey. About one fifth lacked the primary day-180 observation; modeling cannot prove their unobserved outcomes.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Primary long-term endpoint was any COVID-attributed symptom or death at day 180; clinician diagnosis was secondary. Self-report point-in-time symptom questionnaire and self-report of a clinician diagnosis since the preceding survey. Primary day 180; additional day 90 and 120 assessments. Patient-reported symptoms and diagnosis, not a laboratory surrogate. No established minimal important absolute risk reduction; the efficacy rule was posterior probability above 0.975. A statistical decision threshold is not a patient-important change threshold. Adjusted primary risks 2.9% metformin versus 3.6% placebo; raw symptoms 33 versus 46 at day 180. Raw denominators 1439 and 1544 include missing observations; 1139 and 1251 supplied primary day-180 data. Adjusted risk difference −0.8 percentage points, 95% credible interval −2.2 to 0.6; relative risk 0.79, 0.474 to 1.230. Between-arm posterior probability of efficacy 0.83, below 0.975. Secondary clinician diagnosis adjusted risks 0.7% versus 1.4%; raw 8 versus 18. Secondary absolute difference −0.7 points, credible interval −1.5 to 0.1; relative-risk interval reported 0.155–0.995, posterior probability 0.96. Do not replace the negative primary decision with a positive claim based on a secondary relative-risk interval. Intervals computed on different scales need not have identical boundary behavior. Early-infection prevention; comparison of symptoms versus clinician diagnosis. Does not establish benefit for the primary symptom endpoint; provides a secondary diagnosis signal. Observed results are distinguished from stronger preventive language used by authors; editorial conclusion remains uncertain. Present both the primary failure and secondary signal together.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Safety of special interest, including lactic acidosis and self-reported hypoglycemia; general tolerability was not assessed here. 1439 metformin and 1544 placebo in the modified intention-to-treat set. No lactic acidosis reported; hypoglycemia reported by 2 metformin and 4 placebo recipients. This report does not give a comprehensive treatment-discontinuation analysis for intolerance. Fourteen days of assigned treatment, long-term follow-up to 180 days. These findings do not establish that gastrointestinal adverse effects were absent. Post-randomization exclusions, incomplete follow-up, self-report and low event frequency. Randomization limits baseline confounding; selection after allocation and missing outcomes may reintroduce bias. Protocol supports the long-term endpoint, but model regularization and efficacy threshold were updated after the day-28 analysis; registry appendix emphasizes acute outcomes. Secondary analyses were not multiplicity-adjusted. Primary and absolute secondary intervals include no effect; few diagnoses produce substantial uncertainty. Day-90 placebo symptoms are 52 in Table 2 versus 51 in prose; hypertension is 20.9% in Table 1 versus 2% in prose. Protocol printed p109 describes futility at day180 then §21.7.3 says day90; both wordings retained. Use table-specific numbers and retain discrepancies; neither one changes the primary null decision. Largely previously immune US outpatients with acute infection. Applies to this immediate-release 14-day schedule, not all products or chronic use. The symptom primary endpoint differs from the clinician-diagnosis endpoint in COVID-OUT. Preexisting long COVID was not excluded; fluctuating illness can be missed by point-in-time questions. Do not describe this as a trial of treating established long COVID.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: ACTIV-6 metformin appendix, NCT06042855 under master NCT04885530. Published acute-recovery report and earlier long-term preprint share participants with this report. They are one randomized comparison, not independent replications. Bounded comparison with COVID-OUT, Korean treatment trial and REVIVE; no exhaustive new search. Count the published long-term paper once and supersede its preprint for these estimates. Carolyn Bramante, Thomas Stewart and ACTIV-6 investigators. Multicenter US decentralized platform coordinated through Duke and collaborators. NCATS support and BARDA contract; sponsor participated in design, conduct, analysis and publication. Metformin product identified as Aurobindo; a product name does not itself establish donation. Multiple investigators disclosed outside institutional grants, consulting and other industry relationships. The report does not support a blanket claim of no conflicts or no sponsor role. Published Clinical Infectious Diseases 2026 report, DOI 10.1093/cid/ciag335, superseding the preprint for current estimates. Full published article and current registry records retrieved. Master protocol v12.0 retrieved and Appendix G inspected; its separately referenced SAP was not recovered. Current appendix and master records inspected; this is not an audit of every historic registry revision. No correction or retraction identified in the retrieved current records; internal discrepancies retained above. Retrieved November 3–4, 2026. Independent numerical verification is pending, separate from this source assessment.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: STOP-PASC did not find a significant benefit from a 15-day nirmatrelvir–ritonavir course for its selected long COVID symptoms. The study is relevant to established illness because participants already had persistent symptoms when treatment began. Both groups improved over time, which makes the randomized comparison more informative than a before-and-after story about the active drug alone. Our interpretation is that this regimen did not demonstrate the expected advantage in the enrolled population. The finding does not settle every antiviral, duration, symptom subtype, or possible mechanism. It does challenge a claim that improvement after taking this treatment, by itself, proves a drug effect.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Researchers randomized 155 adults at Stanford to nirmatrelvir plus ritonavir or placebo plus ritonavir. The primary assessment pooled severity across six core symptom groups at ten weeks. Enrollment stopped early after the prespecified futility criterion was reached. This design matters because the control was not simply an inert substitute for every component of the active combination. Our reading keeps the exact comparator in every interpretation. The trial also selected participants according to clinical and medication criteria, so its experience should not be extended to excluded people without further evidence. Randomization supports comparison within the trial; it does not eliminate every question about applicability.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: The primary pooled symptom comparison did not show a significant between-group difference. As an illustrative secondary outcome, the adjusted difference in PROMIS fatigue change was 0.38 points, with a 95% confidence interval from −2.40 to 3.15. Fatigue improved within both groups, but that is not the same as evidence that the active treatment caused greater improvement. Our interpretation gives priority to the comparison the trial was designed to make. The interval also prevents a claim that an exact zero effect has been established. Secondary and exploratory findings need caution because multiple comparisons can generate apparently interesting differences even without a reproducible treatment advantage.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: This was a single-center study, with a smaller sample than planned and a mostly vaccinated population with prolonged symptoms. Taste disturbance differed between groups and could have affected masking of self-reported outcomes. Adverse events and treatment discontinuations were recorded, but a modest trial cannot provide a complete picture of rare harms or risks in excluded patients. Our review therefore keeps harms visible alongside the absence of demonstrated benefit. It also separates study exclusions from medical contraindications: the latter require current product-specific authoritative information and qualified clinical interpretation. There is no dosing recommendation in this review and no inference that a longer course would work.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test metformin or UDCA for recovery from established PASC. Metformin versus placebo was the powered primary comparison; UDCA was exploratory. Recovery defined by crossing below a symptom-index threshold at week 8. This is treatment, unlike acute-infection prevention trials. No demonstrated clinical advantage over placebo for this regimen and population. Longer treatment, severe phenotypes and durable function remain unanswered. Better phenotyping, complete outcome reporting and longer, independently replicated trials could change the conclusion. Do not recommend UDCA or metformin based on improvements shared with placebo.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Adults at least 19 with a previous positive test and PASC index at least 12; median age 36, 72% women, 97% vaccinated. Two Seoul tertiary hospitals, infection 30–730 days earlier; upper limit expanded from 180 days during study. 396 randomized, 132 per arm; abstract says 666 screened and Results says 658. Preserve the screening discrepancy without changing the unambiguous randomized counts. Oral metformin plus UDCA placebo. Metformin titrated to 1500 mg/day for 14 days; exact formulation and daily steps deferred to inaccessible protocol. Other arm received UDCA 900 mg/day plus metformin placebo; control received both placebos. Visits weeks 1, 2, 4 and 8. Do not infer the formulation from COVID-OUT or another trial. Double placebo. 1:1:1 parallel allocation. Full sequence generation and concealment details are in the separately linked protocol, unavailable here. Participants, investigators and outcome assessors blinded. Enrollment July 2024–January 2025; follow-up completed April 2025. The report supports randomization but not an invented concealment mechanism. Detailed withdrawal flow and week-8 missing outcome counts require the linked supplement/figure data not fully acquired. Sensitivity analyses for missing week-8 recovery and gray-zone scores described, but exact rules not independently reproduced. Detailed adherence information deferred to protocol. Two placebo participants lacked baseline PASC scores. Intention-to-treat, all 396 randomized, for efficacy; at least one dose for safety. Individual participant; repeated visits and cytokines are not additional people. The common efficacy denominator should not be reused silently for the smaller safety set.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Primary PASC recovery at 8 weeks; continuous score, individual symptoms and cytokines secondary. Weighted 12-domain index, range 0–34. Week 8 primary, weeks 2 and 4 additional. Patient-reported symptom index; cytokines are mechanistic surrogates. Recovery threshold below 12 is a classification threshold, not established complete symptom resolution; design targeted 15 percentage points. A participant can cross the threshold while remaining symptomatic. Recovery 84/132 metformin, 90/132 placebo and 90/132 UDCA. Metformin 63.6%, placebo 68.2%. Metformin-placebo difference −4.55 percentage points, 95% CI −15.98 to 6.88. Score change −10.05 metformin versus −10.43 placebo; between-arm difference 0.38 points. Score difference CI −1.42 to 2.18; within-arm improvement is not treatment efficacy. The primary comparison shows no demonstrated benefit, with uncertainty spanning modest benefit and harm. Established long-COVID treatment. Contradicts a claim that this two-week course improves week-8 recovery. Authors conclude no significant improvement; observed estimates support that bounded statement. Do not substitute preventive trial results for this treatment result.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Adverse events, serious events, hospitalizations and deaths assessed in those taking at least one dose. Main report gives safety percentages but not all exact exposed denominators; do not infer denominators from rounding. Any AE: 7 metformin (5.4%), 6 UDCA (4.6%), 3 placebo (2.3%); no metformin/UDCA serious events; one unrelated placebo arm fracture; no deaths. Event-specific withdrawals are in unavailable Supplement Table 7. Eight-week follow-up after 14-day treatment. Mostly mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal events; sample and duration limit uncommon-harm detection. Blinding and randomization strengths; short treatment, selected younger volunteers, uncertain missing-data detail and threshold-based endpoint limitations. Baseline similarity limits measured confounding; selection limits external validity. Full protocol/SAP comparison remains unavailable despite public main-text access. Secondary cytokine and symptom comparisons unadjusted for multiplicity. Placebo recovery 68.2% greatly exceeded assumed 15%; primary CI excludes the targeted 15-point benefit but not smaller benefit. Abstract screening 666 versus Results 658; Discussion describes 70–80% recovery while main ITT recovery is 66.7%. Record these differences rather than silently harmonizing them. Younger mostly vaccinated adults with generally mild PASC. Two-week oral metformin course only. Week-8 threshold recovery does not establish complete functional recovery or long-term trajectory. Limited applicability to severe, persistent or differently defined long COVID. A null trial of this regimen does not prove all possible regimens ineffective.

So Yun Lim, Jacob Lee, Sung-Han Kim and colleagues. Asan Medical Center and Hallym University Kangnam Sacred Heart Hospital, Seoul. No correction/retraction identified in current article/metadata; screening discrepancy retained. Publisher accessed November 3; assessment November 4, 2026. sections.title: Retraction and replacement
sections.paragraph: The original report was retracted and replaced. The actual notice and replacement were acquired. The original omitted a dose modification and a futility stop. Use REVIVE-REPLACEMENT (DOI 10.7326/ANNALS-26-02144) for the separately assessed report; the original is excluded from efficacy claims.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test adjunctive metformin in Parkinson disease receiving levodopa/carbidopa. The report identifies UPDRS improvement as primary and circulating biomarkers as secondary; registration NCT05781711 is given. Clinical symptom improvement, with biological hypotheses evaluated separately. A biomarker finding cannot replace the primary clinical comparison. This pilot does not establish metformin as an effective Parkinson treatment. Longer-term clinical benefit, tolerability in broader populations and biomarker meaning remain uncertain. Larger blinded trials with intention-to-treat estimates, complete harms and clinically important effect thresholds could change this view. No personal dosing recommendation follows from the pilot.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Human adults at least 50 years old with diagnosed Parkinson disease. Single Tanta University outpatient center in Egypt; diabetes, atypical/secondary parkinsonism and several comorbidities excluded. 60 randomized, 30 per arm; 27 metformin and 25 control analyzed after withdrawals. The pilot population is narrower than all people with Parkinson disease. Glucophage metformin tablets, Mina Pharm, Egypt. Oral 500 mg twice daily for 3 months. Both arms received levodopa/carbidopa 250/25 mg three times daily; unnecessary medicines stopped beforehand. Clinical and blood measurements at baseline and month 3. This tests addition to symptomatic treatment, not replacement of that treatment. Levodopa/carbidopa plus placebo. Parallel allocation, 30 participants per arm. Computer-generated random sequence with permuted blocks; an unblinded pharmacist supplied treatment. Participants and medical professionals blinded; pharmacist not involved in outcome assessment. Recruitment June 2023-August 2024, with 3-month individual follow-up. The report does not fully describe block sizes or every concealment safeguard. Five control participants needed additional amantadine; two metformin participants changed to combined treatment and one did not attend. Withdrawals were excluded rather than imputed. Pill counts and calls every 2 weeks monitored adherence; seven consecutive days off treatment triggered withdrawal. Clinical deterioration and treatment changes led to outcome-related exclusions. Per-protocol analysis of 52 completers. Individual participants; repeated blood markers and scores are not independent participants. Outcome-related attrition weakens the randomized comparison and may bias either direction.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: UPDRS improvement primary; TLR4, BDNF, HMGB1 and alpha-synuclein secondary. UPDRS total/subscales, Hoehn-Yahr and Schwab-England; serum ELISA assays. Baseline and 3 months. Clinical symptom/function measures versus circulating surrogate biomarkers. No prespecified minimal clinically important between-group difference is supplied. Disease modification was not directly established by the design. UPDRS median (IQR): metformin 152 (129-166) to 128 (98-151); control 141 (115-164) to 139 (101-151.5). Outcome denominators were 27 metformin and 25 control. Post-treatment rank-biserial correlation r=0.106; between-arm P=0.515 for total UPDRS. Within-metformin P=0.001 does not demonstrate superiority. All listed clinical post-treatment between-arm comparisons were nonsignificant. Confidence intervals for the between-arm clinical effect are not supplied. Table 3 labels all four serum markers ng/mL; reported post-treatment between-arm P values are 0.03 for alpha-synuclein, 0.02 BDNF, 0.03 HMGB1 and 0.04 TLR4. They do not prove clinical benefit. Parkinson clinical benefit and biomarker hypotheses. Supports reported biomarker differences; does not demonstrate superior clinical UPDRS outcomes or disease modification. The authors acknowledge no significant between-group UPDRS difference; the editorial conclusion agrees and rejects within-arm efficacy inference. Replace vague pending placeholders with this distinction.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Participants queried for adverse effects at visits and calls every 2 weeks. Table 4 reports 27 metformin and 25 control completers, not all 60 randomized participants. Metformin/control counts: nausea 6/5, diarrhea 4/2, vomiting 5/3, hypotension 9/5, delusions 5/3, abdominal pain 8/5. The described withdrawals mainly involved clinical progression or treatment changes; systematic graded safety data for all randomized participants are not provided. Three months. Nonsignificant safety comparisons in this small completer sample do not establish equivalent safety. Small single-center pilot, completer exclusions and limited concealment detail. Randomization reduces initial confounding, but post-randomization exclusions and uncontrolled diet/metabolic factors remain. The current NCT05781711 record agrees on 3-month UPDRS and secondary biomarkers; historical versions were not available in this packet. Numerous clinical subscale and biomarker tests without a described multiplicity correction. Small sample and no clinical effect CI limit exclusion of clinically relevant effects. BDNF within-arm P is 0.003 in Table 3 but 0.0003 in prose; baseline ALT/AST P values also differ between prose and Table 1. Preserve table-specific numbers and these discrepancies; do not choose the more favorable P value. Older adults without diabetes on levodopa/carbidopa at one Egyptian center. One oral dose and one 3-month duration, not all metformin regimens or formulations. Symptom scores and blood biomarkers do not establish slower long-term progression. No demonstrated clinical superiority; external applicability and durability uncertain. A mechanistic rationale remains hypothesis-generating.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Explore TCA metabolites, hippocampal connectivity and cognitive change after adjunctive metformin. Explicitly post hoc exploratory analysis. A proposed biological explanation of an existing trial signal, not a fresh efficacy test. Preserve exploratory status. Exploratory biological changes merit further study but do not prove a treatment mechanism. Causality, reproducibility and relation to everyday function remain unknown. Preregistered replicated mediator analyses with clinical outcomes and direct metabolic measurements are needed. Keep this report in the same family as the parent.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Human schizophrenia participants from the parent cohort, median age 22. Stable illness and antipsychotic treatment; selected available plasma and follow-up. Parent 72; metabolite analysis 58, 40 metformin and 18 control; final MRI 33, 21 and 12. Biomarker and imaging subsets are smaller than the randomized trial. Metformin tablets as in the parent report. Up to 500 mg three times daily orally, or maximum tolerated dose. Stable antipsychotics, doses converted to chlorpromazine equivalents. Baseline, 12 and 24 weeks. Use the parent for the product and titration history. Antipsychotics alone. Inherited 2:1 randomized parent allocation. Computer random-number generator in parent. Open-label treatment; trained evaluators, parent cognitive evaluator masked. Samples collected in the September 2017–April 2021 parent trial. Post hoc sample availability is not randomized. 14 parent participants absent from plasma analysis; MRI selected 41 then excluded eight after preprocessing. Last observation carried forward for missing TCA/cognition; sensitivity analysis on observed and imputed data; MRI not imputed. Parent reports high pill adherence; no independent biomarker adherence confirmation. Availability and image-quality exclusions; motion threshold 3 mm or 3 degrees in supplement. Post hoc available-case subset of randomized cohort. Participant, not metabolite, brain region, voxel or repeated sample. Selection and imputation can distort association estimates.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Post hoc metabolites and imaging; cognition correlations exploratory. LC-MS/MS for nine plasma metabolites, MCCB and 3-T resting-state fMRI. Weeks 12 and 24. Circulating biomarkers and functional connectivity, not validated surrogates for recovery. No validated clinical benefit threshold for these metabolite/connectivity changes. Plasma concentrations do not directly measure neuronal TCA flux. At week 24 adjusted lactate means 194.34 versus 342.43 micrograms/mL; pyruvate 43.45 versus 81.62. Metabolite analysis 40 versus 18; MRI 21 versus 12. Lactate between-arm difference −148.09 micrograms/mL, CI −184.61 to −111.57; pyruvate −38.17, CI −47.18 to −29.17. Abstract lactate −80.81 and pyruvate −17.51 are within-metformin changes, not between-arm effects. Imaging contrasts −0.334 at week 12 and 0.284 at week 24; exploratory correlations lack multiplicity-adjusted confirmation. This resolves the crucial within-arm versus between-arm distinction. Potential TCA/connectivity explanation of cognitive signal. Indirect mechanistic support only; not independent efficacy evidence. Observations are associations; author interpretation of activation is a hypothesis. Use no clinical-benefit grade from these biomarkers alone.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: No new systematic harms analysis in this mechanistic report. Biomarker subset is not a newly exposed safety cohort. Parent reports decreased appetite; companion cannot independently confirm safety. No new treatment-withdrawal analysis in CP017. Same 24-week exposure window. Absence of safety results here is not absence of adverse events. Post hoc selection, small imaging sample, open-label parent and multiple correlational analyses. Metabolic status, antipsychotic exposure and other factors may confound mediator-outcome associations. Analysis not prospectively specified; current registry cognition primary does not prospectively validate these exploratory tests. Bonferroni used for some metabolite contrasts and FWE for imaging; correlations/interactions deliberately use raw P values. sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Review diabetes drugs as potential sarcopenia therapies. Narrative review; no registered systematic-review protocol reported. Biological rationale and research priorities. Not a randomized treatment study. Mechanistic promise justified trials but was not proof of improved function. Optimal population and net effect remained unknown at publication. Later randomized functional outcomes should update the synthesis. MET-PREVENT now provides such evidence and is assessed separately.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Mixed cells, animals and human populations, many with type 2 diabetes. Heterogeneous settings and definitions of muscle health. No newly recruited or pooled participant population. Do not sum the review's study citations as independent trial participants. Multiple diabetes drug classes, including metformin. Different doses/routes across cited studies; no review-wide regimen. Exercise and other interventions vary. Durations differ by cited source. No universal schedule can be extracted from this review. Various placebo, usual-care and observational comparators. No new allocation. Randomization applies to individual cited trials only. No participant-level blinding in a narrative review. Literature available before publication in 2023. The review itself cannot remove bias from its sources. No participant attrition in the review itself. No complete reproducible search or missing-study analysis. Adherence belongs to underlying trials. Systematic inclusion/exclusion and duplicate-screening process not reported. Narrative selected literature. Individual source study, with potential overlap. Unreported search methods limit confidence that all contradictory studies were included.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: No primary efficacy endpoint for the review. Muscle mass, strength, physical performance and proposed pathways. Varies by underlying study. Mix of clinical function and surrogates. No single meaningful-change threshold across this heterogeneous evidence. Muscle mass and physical function are distinct outcomes. Describes a positive small prefrailty study and blunted training adaptation in MASTERS. No pooled numerator or denominator. No meta-analytic estimate. Direction and context vary; no unified metformin benefit estimate. No review-level confidence interval or formal certainty analysis reported. For guide numbers, use the acquired primary reports rather than copying secondary summaries. Why diabetes drugs were investigated for sarcopenia. Supports rationale and uncertainty, not demonstrated treatment efficacy. Authors call for trials; editorial synthesis includes later negative MET-PREVENT results. A historical review must not outrank a later directly relevant RCT.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Discusses gastrointestinal intolerance, lactic acidosis and class-specific risks. No review-wide exposure denominator. Qualitative safety discussion, not a new comparative safety estimate. No pooled treatment withdrawal count. Variable source durations. Current labels and directly assessed trials take precedence for guide safety facts. Narrative-selection and citation bias possible; heterogeneous designs. Observational diabetes-drug comparisons confounded by indication and health status. No prespecified systematic outcome hierarchy or formal bias assessment. No new inferential tests; selective emphasis across many studies remains possible. No pooled uncertainty estimate. Describes MET-PREVENT as underway; its 2025 results are now available. The forward-looking statement is historical, not a current missing trial. Research rationale for people with or at risk of sarcopenia. Does not identify a proven metformin regimen for those without diabetes. Does not establish benefit on falls, independence or survival. Diabetes observations cannot be transferred directly to frail adults without diabetes. Use as context only.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: Secondary review, no new study family. MASTERS is separately assessed; MET-PREVENT later reports results. Underlying trials must not be counted again through this review. Narrative scope, not an exhaustive updated search. Source count is not independent-study count. Miles Witham, Avan Sayer and colleagues. Geriatrics and muscle-research collaborators. No specific review funding; several authors acknowledge NIHR Newcastle Biomedical Research Centre support. No trial products supplied for this review. Witham and Sayer disclose being MET-PREVENT investigators. Retain that relevant disclosure without treating it as proof of bias. Published Drugs & Aging 2023, DOI 10.1007/s40266-023-01042-4. Full article acquired and relevant metformin sections assessed. No necessary separate meta-analysis dataset identified. No registered systematic-review protocol reported. No correction/retraction identified in retrieved records; time-sensitive trial-status statements superseded. November 3–4, 2026. This assessment is limited to its use as metformin background, not every drug class discussed.

questionAnswers.question: How could the design or analysis mislead?
questionAnswers.answer: Tumoroid samples miss tumor heterogeneity and key stromal/immune/vascular components; culture conditions affect representativeness (pp. 2–3). Many natural compounds limited by bioavailability/stability; small or absent clinical studies, variable toxicity and uncertain optimal dosing (pp. 5–18). Effective laboratory concentrations may not be achievable clinically; higher doses/drug interactions risk off-target effects and adverse events (p. 20). Nanocarrier long-term toxicity and safety remain unknown for many materials; limited clinical translation (p. 20). Cancer-specific molecular context, pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics and robust clinical trials needed; intellectual-property/regulatory/funding hurdles (pp. 20, 24).

sections.title: Stated limitations
sections.paragraph: Only fingolimod and interferon-beta treated datasets available; low DEG thresholds; restricted proteome validation; no basic or clinical trials of highlighted candidates (PDFp14). The complete pathway-drug supplementary lists are referenced but not printed in this supplied PDF (p15). Dense raster Figure4 labels include unresolved research identifiers; candidate enumeration is incomplete and held for visual reconciliation.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Prevent severe acute COVID-19 with early outpatient medication. Prespecified composite through day 14. Hypoxemia, emergency visit, hospitalization or death. Secondary endpoints do not replace the primary. Early metformin did not significantly reduce the original primary composite. Whether secondary benefits generalize remains uncertain. Independent current-population trials with prespecified clinical endpoints matter. Guide separates this from long-COVID prevention.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Adults 30–85 with overweight or obesity and recent COVID-19. Six US institutions, remote enrollment; positive test within three days and symptoms within seven. 1431 randomized; 1323 mITT: 663 metformin, 660 control; 52.2% vaccinated. Median age 46; limited applicability to current immune backgrounds. Immediate-release metformin. Oral escalation to 1500 mg/day over six days, 14 days total. Factorial fluvoxamine, ivermectin or matched placebo assignments. Primary day 14; hospitalization/death also day 28. No comparison of IR versus ER. Concurrent matched placebo for metformin. Equal probability among open groups, site-stratified. Pregenerated mass-weighted urn sequence. Blinded participants, clinicians and outcome assessors; similar pill burden. December 2020–January 2022, with factorial expansion May 2021. Comparisons between different drugs’ crude rates are invalid because enrollment periods differ. 108 excluded from mITT because no trial drug received. Primary follow-up missing about 1.4%; symptom diary missing about 25%. Drug discontinuation recorded; current registry contains six factorial-arm counts. ITT sensitivity analyses described separately from mITT. mITT with multiple imputation; symptoms not imputed. Individual participant. Factorial arms are not independent trials.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Primary four-part composite; health-care component and symptoms secondary. Home oxygen saturation, medical-record verification and symptom diaries. Day 14 primary. Composite mixes a noisy physiologic measure with major clinical events. Planned 35% relative reduction, not a validated universal MCID. Oximeter limitations weaken the endpoint but do not justify retrospectively calling the trial primary-positive. Primary 154/652 metformin versus 179/653 control; emergency visit/hospitalization/death 27/652 versus 48/655. Full mITT denominators 663/660; displayed event fractions are observed complete cases. Adjusted primary OR .84, 95% CI .66–1.09, P=.19. Secondary health-care composite OR .58, CI .35–.94; day-14 hospitalization/death OR .47, CI .20–1.11. Day-28 hospitalization/death 8/596 versus 19/601; secondary CIs not adjusted for multiplicity. No primary benefit demonstrated; secondary signals warrant further testing. Acute severity and symptom claims. Primary null; secondary clinical benefit signal. Authors’ cautious primary conclusion is retained despite stronger later commentary. No claim of proven general antiviral replacement.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Non-COVID events solicited through day 14; serious events through day 28 in registry. Registry six-arm safety populations total 1323. No medication-related serious event reported; one all-cause death occurred in a metformin/ivermectin recipient. Metformin-only discontinuations 56/284 versus double-placebo 49/295; combination-arm counts differ. Short treatment and acute follow-up. These arm-specific discontinuations are not the entire factorial metformin effect. Remote oximetry, mITT exclusions and missing symptom diaries. Concurrent randomization and adjusted co-medication/vaccination analyses reduce confounding. Registered protocol/SAP recovered; report explicitly identifies secondary analyses. No multiplicity correction for secondary outcomes. Hospitalization/death events rare with wide intervals. Wording about symptom reduction is awkward in Results; figures and conclusion indicate no symptom benefit. Use the explicit conclusion and endpoint hierarchy. Early acute outpatient infection in overweight/obese adults. Fourteen-day IR course. Not established long-COVID treatment or a comparison with authorized antivirals. Variants, vaccination and enrollment criteria limit extrapolation. Long-term follow-up is a separate outcome in the same trial.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: COVID-OUT randomized family. P-COVIDOUT-2023 long-term and MF-COVID-VIRAL-2024 virologic reports. Overlapping participants; count once. Current inventory and linked registry. Multiple reports increase outcome detail, not independent replication. Carolyn Bramante and COVID-OUT collaborators. US investigator-led multicenter remote trial. Parsemus, Rainwater, Fast Grants and UnitedHealth Group Foundation; stated no funder role. Apotex fluvoxamine placebo; Edenbridge ivermectin active/placebo; metformin donor not established here. Separate original NEJM disclosure forms not recovered; later related report provides named investigator disclosures. Do not substitute later disclosures for exact original forms. NEJM 2022, DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2201662. Full text, tables and current trial record inspected. Protocol/SAP recovered; original acute supplement not fully audited. NCT04510194. Long-term 2023 correction belongs to the companion report, not an acute primary-result correction. November 3–4, 2026. Preserve report-specific version history.

Final primary population hormone-receptor positive after planned futility assessment of receptor-negative disease. Recurrence, new invasive cancer or death. Subgroup analyses cannot replace the primary result. Metformin did not improve invasive disease-free survival in the primary population. sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Adults 18–74 with high-risk nonmetastatic breast cancer without diabetes. Canada, US, UK and Switzerland; complete resection and standard cancer therapy. 3649 randomized: 1824 metformin and 1825 placebo; primary ER/PgR-positive group 1268 and 1265. Almost all participants were women. Apotex metformin and matching placebo. Oral 850 mg daily for four weeks then twice daily, intended five years. Standard endocrine, chemotherapy, radiation and targeted therapy as indicated. Median primary follow-up 96.2 months. Not metformin monotherapy for cancer. Identical-appearing placebo. 1:1 minimization, balanced by center and stratified by receptors, BMI and chemotherapy. Computer-based allocation procedure described as minimization with equal probabilities. Double-blind. Concurrent enrollment 2010–2013, data cutoff October 2020. Randomization and long follow-up are major strengths. All randomized participants included in assigned-group analyses. Missing dates imputed within known intervals; time-to-event censoring used. Final-year reported continuation 64.3% metformin versus 70.9% placebo in the defined eligible subset. Receptor-negative participants stopped study drug for futility while blinded follow-up continued. ITT, with prespecified/supervised change in primary population. Individual participant. Discontinuation affects exposure but does not create a second trial.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Primary invasive disease-free survival; OS and recurrence endpoints secondary. Centrally verified events and time-to-event analysis. Final follow-up approximately eight years. Clinical cancer outcomes. Design targeted about four percentage points at five years, based on investigator consensus. Metabolic improvements are not the same endpoint. sections.title: Limits

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Measure weight and metabolic effects of metformin and possible SNP modification. Planned companion analyses; primary parent endpoint was invasive disease-free survival. Six-month metabolic response. This report predates the definitive cancer-outcome report. Improved insulin and weight measures did not establish improved cancer outcomes. Mechanistic mediation and selected subgroups require direct testing. Clinical outcomes, not biomarker changes alone, could change treatment conclusions. One trial can improve biomarkers while failing its clinical endpoint.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Nondiabetic adults with high-risk operable breast cancer. International MA.32 participants still taking study drug with paired fasting bloods. 3649 randomized; metabolic subset 2915: 1412 metformin, 1503 placebo; SNP subset 2747. 734 randomized participants are absent from the metabolic cohort. Metformin 850 mg caplets; matching placebo. Once daily for four weeks then twice daily; intended five years. Standard surgery and systemic/radiation cancer therapies. Baseline to six months in this analysis. Different follow-up from the final cancer trial. Placebo. Parent 1:1 assignment. Computer-generated randomization. Double-blind; laboratory assays blinded to allocation. Paired baseline and on-treatment sampling. Selection after randomization limits a simple ITT interpretation. Postrandomization exclusion of those without paired on-treatment samples. More metformin-assigned and Black participants excluded; diet/activity missing in over 75%. Required on-drug status, but short-term dosing compliance uncertain. 412 metformin and 322 placebo excluded from metabolic cohort. Available paired samples, not full randomized ITT. Individual participant. Selection may distort effect magnitude and generalizability.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Weight, glucose, insulin, HOMA, leptin, hsCRP; interaction analyses. Central insulin/leptin/hsCRP assays with 10% repeats; local glucose. Six months. Intermediate metabolic measures, not cancer recurrence. Clinical-benefit thresholds not established for these changes. No surrogate validation for anticancer benefit. Median weight change −1.4 kg versus +.5 kg. Weight-change n=1394 versus 1499; metabolic subset n=1412/1503. Adjusted metformin/placebo ratios: insulin .85, HOMA .83, leptin .80, hsCRP .84. Weight standardized ratio .97, CI .97–.98; ratios adjust baseline, age and BMI. Reported P<.0001 for these comparisons; no qualitative SNP interaction. Raw within-arm percentages and adjusted between-arm ratios are different quantities. Biomarkers versus cancer outcomes. Metabolic improvement supported, anticancer benefit not established. Authors anticipated possible clinical benefit; later primary report was negative. Do not preserve an outdated “outcomes forthcoming” statement.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: No new comprehensive safety analysis in this paper. Selected metabolic cohort is not an unbiased safety denominator. Authors state toxicity/compliance data were unavailable until efficacy analysis. Drug-related discontinuation may contribute to exclusions. Six-month biomarker window. Use the later parent report for harms, retaining its numerical discrepancies. Conditioning on on-treatment samples and multiple biomarkers. Randomization helps, but selection and unmeasured lifestyle changes remain. Parent primary clinical endpoint explicitly deferred. Multiple biomarker and interaction tests without a stated family-wise correction. Large biomarker sample, but no clinical-outcome estimate here. Printed HOMA formula units are inconsistent with conventional dimensional form; do not use it as a calculation instruction. Metabolic findings cannot validate a cancer-prevention claim. Selected nondiabetic breast-cancer population. 1700 mg/day after ramp-up. Supports metabolic change in this setting. Not evidence of survival benefit, healthy-person longevity or a validated genetic prescribing rule. Later clinical results take precedence for clinical claims.

Do not count as an independent positive cancer trial. Pamela Goodwin, Bingshu Chen, Marguerite Ennis and colleagues. CCTG and central Toronto laboratories. Public/cancer-charity support; statement of no sponsor role in this report. Apotex in-kind metformin/placebo. Roche employment and several oncology-industry grants/honoraria disclosed. Funding statements are report-specific. npj Breast Cancer 2021, DOI 10.1038/s41523-021-00275-z. Full XML and supplements acquired. No correction identified in retrieved records; clinical follow-up published in 2022. November 3–4, 2026. Corrects the earlier mistaken classification of these files as protocol/SAP.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test adding metformin to gemcitabine and erlotinib. Prespecified six-month overall survival. Clinical survival benefit in advanced pancreatic cancer. Mechanistic hypotheses are secondary. This regimen did not improve survival. Small effects, different regimens and biologically selected groups remain separate questions. Adequately powered randomized clinical outcome trials would be needed. Not a reason to change prescribed diabetes care without clinical review.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Adults with advanced pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Four Dutch centers; approximately 73% metastatic; diabetes allowed. 121 randomized: 60 metformin and 61 placebo; diabetes in six and eight respectively. Not a prevention study. Oral metformin tablets. 500 mg twice daily in week one, then 1000 mg twice daily until progression or intolerance. Gemcitabine 1000 mg/m² on days 1, 8 and 15 every 28 days plus erlotinib 100 mg daily. Median follow-up 28.1 months. Not representative of every current pancreatic regimen. Matched placebo with identical cancer treatment. Central TENALEA allocation, stratified by hospital, diabetes and stage. Computer-generated blocks of six; block size concealed. Patients, physicians and study personnel masked. Concurrent randomized phase II comparison. Good allocation safeguards support the null comparison. Follow-up continued after drug discontinuation. Serial plasma analysis available in selected participants, including 29 metformin recipients. Full-dose escalation in 38/60 metformin versus 49/61 placebo; dose reductions 34 versus 17. No reported postrandomization efficacy exclusion from ITT. Randomized ITT efficacy; selected biomarker subsets. Individual patient. Drug-concentration subgroups are not randomized dose comparisons.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Primary six-month overall survival; PFS, response and metabolic analyses secondary. Survival follow-up and RECIST response; CTCAE toxicity. Primary six months. Clinical endpoints; insulin and drug concentrations exploratory. Design sought a very large six-month survival change from 50% to 75%. Power does not establish a small-effect equivalence margin. Six-month survival 56.7% metformin versus 63.9% placebo. 60 versus 61 randomized; 52 versus 54 deaths over follow-up. Median survival 6.8 versus 7.6 months; HR 1.056, 95% CI .72–1.55. Six-month difference −7.2 percentage points, calculated from rounded estimates. Six-month P=.41; overall HR P=.78; PFS HR 1.18, CI .77–1.82. No demonstrated survival advantage. Metformin as cancer treatment add-on. Contradicts expected major survival benefit. Trial data are null; mitochondrial or insulin explanations remain hypotheses. Do not imply a responsive high-dose subgroup was proven.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Graded treatment-emergent adverse events. 60 metformin and 61 placebo assigned. Grade 3/4 neutropenia 15 each; diarrhea six versus three; fatigue six versus two; no hypoglycemia reported. All study drugs stopped for toxicity in 13 versus eight; one metformin-only GI withdrawal and four metformin/erlotinib GI withdrawals. Median treatment 2.5 versus 4.6 months. Shorter exposure in metformin complicates direct toxicity-frequency interpretation. Small phase II trial with good masking; limited exposure and dose reductions. More performance-status-2 participants and higher CA19-9 in metformin arm; adjusted survival remained null. Separate protocol/SAP not acquired for historical endpoint comparison. Biomarker and concentration analyses exploratory and multiple. Wide HR interval permits moderate benefit or harm. One Results sentence calls placebo n=60; randomization figure and total establish 61. Preserve the discrepancy; use coherent randomized denominators. Advanced pancreatic cancer, including a small diabetic subgroup. This chemotherapy combination and conventional antidiabetic doses. Does not support a survival benefit as an add-on. Not all cancers, preventive settings or future combinations. Post hoc high-concentration survival cannot justify dose escalation.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: Kordes pancreatic phase II trial. Biomarker analyses are within this trial. No additional independent trial from serial drug measurements. Current guide sources only. One randomized family. Sil Kordes, Michael Pollak, Johanna Wilmink and colleagues. Academic Medical Centre and other Dutch hospitals. Academic Medical Centre and Terry Fox Foundation; stated no funder role. Commercial product supply details not confirmed in inspected text. Authors declared no competing interests. Disclosure does not substitute for design appraisal. Lancet Oncology 2015, DOI 10.1016/S1470-2045(15)00027-3. Full report acquired from author-associated institutional source. Separate protocol and appendices not recovered. NCT01210911 identified in report. No correction/retraction identified in retrieved records. November 3–4, 2026. Primary results directly inspected.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Review lactic acidosis risk in metformin users with impaired kidney function. Published search criteria; no review registration reported. Safety and possible prescribing-policy change. This is a 2014 review, not current labeling. Kidney function and acute illness are central to safe use. Rare-event risk in severe CKD remained uncertain in this review. Current high-quality safety data and updated labeling govern present clinical decisions. Do not individualize dose from this historical article.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Human type 2 diabetes/CKD studies. MEDLINE and Cochrane, English-language January 1950–June 2014. 818 records to 65 reports: ten pharmacokinetic, twenty case series, thirty-one observational/surveillance, three meta-analyses and one trial. Report counts are not unique participant counts. Metformin; formulations/doses varied across studies. Oral clinical use and pharmacokinetic exposure. Other glucose-lowering treatment and concurrent illnesses varied. Heterogeneous study periods and follow-up. No single regimen or exposure is tested by this review. Other therapies, nonuse or kidney-function strata depending on study. Review-level study selection, not patient allocation. Predominantly nonrandomized evidence. No common masking method across included designs. Search completed July 2014. Observational associations cannot establish causal safety equivalence. Study-level attrition varied and was not pooled. Kidney function missing in more than 25% in one large cited cohort. Prescribing records do not ensure ingestion. Excluded small case series, nonhuman studies and non-English evidence. Narrative synthesis of heterogeneous reports. Primary study or cohort; overlapping databases possible. No de novo unique-person denominator.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Lactic acidosis, lactate, metformin levels and clinical outcomes. Definitions varied; some code-based, some laboratory-confirmed. Person-year incidence in cohorts; short pharmacokinetic sampling. Serious clinical harm versus intermediate lactate elevations. Lactic acidosis definition: lactate above 5 mmol/L and pH below 7.35. Elevated lactate alone is not the same event. Typical reported rates around 3–10 per 100,000 person-years; some higher. Cited meta-analysis: zero events over 70,490 metformin and 55,451 comparator person-years. Upper 95% incidence limits 4.3 and 5.4 per 100,000 person-years. Observational estimates conflict; one CKD analysis HR 6.37, CI 1.48–27.5. Sparse events and broad CIs limit conclusions for impaired kidneys. Zero observed events is not zero risk. Rare-harm interpretation and renal clearance. Contextual support, not authority to override current contraindications. Authors proposed expanded access; guide uses current FDA-label thresholds. No unsupported reassurance of zero acidosis risk.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Clinical codes, spontaneous reports and laboratory diagnoses varied. No unified exposed denominator across 65 reports. Rare but potentially fatal acidosis; competing acute illness often present. No pooled withdrawal result. Study-specific durations. Detection and attribution are substantial limitations. Confounding by indication, healthier-user selection and surveillance bias. Acute kidney injury, sepsis and hypoxia can cause both metformin accumulation and acidosis. Supplementary PRISMA details not separately acquired; no historical protocol audit. Narrative review, not a new pooled causal estimate. Rare-event estimates unstable in severe CKD. 2014 creatinine-based FDA restrictions and proposed dosing table are historical, not current policy. Do not copy old prescribing rules into the guide. Diabetes with CKD, not healthy longevity use. Clinical metformin exposure; no evidence for experimental high-dose use. Supports kidney-function monitoring and contextualizes rare harm. Cannot establish safety during acute illness or eGFR below current contraindication threshold. Current product labeling supplies current precautions.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: Systematic review of mixed designs. Some shared national databases and nested reviews. Overlap must not be counted as independent trials. Search scope fixed at June 2014. Not a comprehensive 2026 safety update. Silvio Inzucchi, Kasia Lipska, Helen Mayo, Clifford Bailey and Darren McGuire. Academic diabetes/clinical research authors. Investigator NIH/Yale support disclosed; no new trial funded. No product administration by reviewers. Multiple consulting, honoraria, travel and industry relationships disclosed. Disclosures do not determine the scientific conclusion. JAMA 2014 systematic review. Full text acquired. Separate supplemental flow diagram not acquired. Review protocol registration not reported. No correction identified in retrieved records; regulatory statements superseded by current labels. November 3–4, 2026. Use only as dated historical safety context.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test low-dose metformin against recurrence of colorectal adenomas and polyps. Coprimary number and prevalence at one year. Post-polypectomy lesion recurrence. Not colorectal cancer incidence or mortality. A small blinded trial is encouraging for recurrent lesions. Durability, generalizability, rare harms and cancer outcomes remain uncertain. Larger independent long-term randomized trials with cancer outcomes could strengthen the case. Do not recommend self-treatment or reduced surveillance.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Nondiabetic adults aged 40–80 after polypectomy. Five Japanese hospitals; excluded regular NSAIDs, hereditary syndromes and major organ disease. 498 screened; 151 randomized, 79 metformin and 72 placebo; 133 follow-up colonoscopies, 71 and 62. About 70% had multiple or advanced adenomas at baseline. Metformin tablets versus lactose placebo. Oral 250 mg once daily after breakfast for one year. Prior polypectomy; surveillance colonoscopy. One year. This unusually low research dose is not a prescribing recommendation. Identical placebo. Central stratification by hospital, age, sex and BMI. Computer-generated random allocation. Patients, clinicians, endoscopists and investigators masked. Concurrent 2011–2014 recruitment. Experienced endoscopists and masked video review strengthen outcome ascertainment. Eight metformin and ten placebo lacked follow-up colonoscopy. Complete-case outcome analysis despite ITT terminology. Median compliance 91% versus 92%; nobody removed for under-80% adherence. 347 excluded before randomization, including 183 with concern about incomplete baseline clearance. 133 with follow-up colonoscopy. Individual participant; multiple lesions are not extra patients. Missing outcome bias remains possible.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Coprimary lesion count and prevalence; metabolic measures secondary. Colonoscopy, three-expert video review and pathology. One-year repeat examination. Adenoma/polyp recurrence is an intermediate cancer-risk endpoint. No established patient-important threshold for one-year lesion reduction. Adenoma reduction is not itself cancer prevention. Any polyp 27/71 metformin versus 35/62 placebo; adenoma 22/71 versus 32/62. Observed colonoscopy denominators 71 and 62, not all 151 randomized. Polyp RR .67, 95% CI .47–.97; adenoma RR .60, CI .39–.92. Any-polyp prevalence 38.0% versus 56.5%; median polyp count zero versus one. P=.034 for polyp prevalence, .016 for adenoma prevalence; count comparisons P=.041 and .037. Adenoma percentage printed as 30.6% does not reproduce 22/71; retain counts and reported RR. Adenoma recurrence versus colorectal cancer prevention. Supports a preliminary lesion-reduction signal; cancer prevention remains unproven. Authors’ broader chemoprevention interpretation exceeds the measured one-year cancer outcomes. No colorectal cancers detected at follow-up does not prove prevention.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: NCI-CTCAE version 4.0 grading during follow-up. Safety table uses 71 and 62 completers. Six metformin and nine placebo events listed, all grade 1; diarrhea one versus four; no serious events reported. One placebo discontinuation for diarrhea. One year. Small size and completer safety denominator cannot establish absence of rare harm. Small regional trial, incomplete colonoscopy follow-up and possible missed baseline lesions. Randomization limits confounding; post hoc insulin-resistance groups are not randomized. Separately published 2012 protocol not acquired in this packet. Multiple coprimary/count/metabolic tests without a reported multiplicity adjustment. Modest event counts, confidence intervals near no effect. Reported adenoma 30.6% differs from 22/71; claimed ITT actually depends on observed follow-up. HOMA-IR subgroup interaction P=.141 does not prove a predictive responder marker. Selected Japanese nondiabetic post-polypectomy adults. 250 mg/day, one year. Supports possible reduction in recurrent lesions. Not average-risk adults, longer-term cancer prevention, cancer treatment or all doses. Surveillance remains a separate established care question.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: Higurashi 2016 randomized trial. Hosono 2010 crypt-foci pilot is a separate earlier study. Distinct participants; same research lineage does not mean independent replication of cancer outcomes. Current guide inventory only. Do not pool crypt foci, adenomas and cancer as one outcome. Takuma Higurashi, Atsushi Nakajima and colleagues. Five Japanese hospitals. Japanese Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare cancer-research grant; stated no funder role. Drugs purchased from Dainippon Sumitomo and Kokando. Authors declared no competing interests. Purchased products are not described as donated. Lancet Oncology 2016, DOI 10.1016/S1470-2045(15)00565-3. Full nine-page article acquired and read. Separate protocol and any additional appendix not recovered. UMIN000006254 identified. No correction/retraction identified in retrieved records. November 3–4, 2026. The numerical discrepancy remains visible in the assessment.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test concurrent and maintenance metformin with chemoradiation. Primary one-year treatment-failure proportion. Failure includes progression, death or discontinuation of trial treatment/evaluations. This endpoint is not conventional PFS. This small trial raises a meaningful warning about this combination. Exact contribution of toxicity, treatment interruption and baseline imbalance is uncertain. Any future regimen requires direct controlled efficacy and safety evidence. The trial does not justify general claims that metformin promotes all cancers.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Adults with unresected stage III NSCLC without diabetes. Seven Canadian institutions. 54 randomized: 26 metformin, 28 control; one per arm withdrew before treatment. Accrual was below the planned approximately 96 participants. Metformin supplied as oral study medication. Escalated to 2000 mg/day during chemoradiation, then up to 12 months. Platinum chemotherapy, mainly cisplatin/etoposide, plus 60–63 Gy radiation; later amendments allowed consolidation and durvalumab. Primary 12 months, survival follow-up to 24 months. Regimen differs from NRG-LU001. Chemoradiation without metformin. Central OCOG randomization, stratified by stage and later consolidation chemotherapy. Sequence-generation detail not fully provided in main report. Open-label; outcome adjudication committee masked. Recruitment 2014–2019; stopped for slow accrual. Stopping for accrual is distinct from an efficacy stopping rule. One pre-treatment withdrawal per arm; discontinuation counted in primary failure. Composite chosen partly to reduce informative censoring from inability to return. Only six completed one year of metformin. No randomized participant excluded from efficacy ITT. 54 for efficacy; 52 started treatment. Individual patient. Primary composite captures feasibility, while survival analyses answer separate questions.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Primary binary failure; conventional PFS/OS secondary. CT imaging and clinical evaluation; CTCAE 4.03 for grade 3+ events. Failure by 12 months. Clinical composite includes treatment feasibility as well as cancer events. No independently validated patient-important threshold for this composite. A discontinuation is not necessarily cancer progression. Failure 18/26 metformin versus 12/28 control. 69.2% versus 42.9%; full randomized denominators. One-year conventional PFS 34.8% versus 63.0%, HR 2.42, CI 1.14–5.10. One-year OS 47.4% versus 85.2%, HR 3.80, CI 1.49–9.73. Wide intervals; primary Fisher P=.05. Reported failure-free difference −26.4 points has CI −51.0 to −0.9 when endpoints are ordered. The unfavorable direction is important despite limited precision. Cancer treatment benefit and harm. Contradicts routine addition; supports highlighting severe toxicity and unfavorable survival. Trial observations do not establish the authors' speculative causal explanations. Do not bury harm under mechanistic enthusiasm.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Only grade 3 or higher adverse events recorded. Table uses randomized denominators 26 and 28 although one per arm never treated. Any grade 3+ AE 14/26 versus 7/28; lung infection six versus zero, esophagitis five versus one; one grade 5 respiratory failure in metformin arm. Metformin stopped for toxicity in three; chemoradiation completion also lower in metformin arm. Most events occurred in first 84 days; follow-up extended beyond treatment. Do not compare these severe-event rates with all-grade rates from other trials. Small, early-closed open-label trial, with masked adjudication. Metformin group had larger mean tumor volumes and fewer durvalumab recipients; chance imbalance may matter. Separate protocol and supplement not acquired; no prespecified stopping rule for accrual or efficacy reported. Several secondary survival comparisons; exploratory results require caution. Intervals wide but unfavorable. Main text sample-size target 94 versus abstract/planned 96; safety denominator differs from stated treated-population approach. Do not claim a proven biological mechanism for harm. Nondiabetic unresected stage III NSCLC under intensive chemoradiation. Mostly cisplatin-based combinations with prolonged metformin. No support for routine anticancer addition; possible harm. Not a test of continuing medically indicated diabetes treatment or all cancer types. Population and regimen boundaries are essential.
