sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test low-dose metformin effects on rectal aberrant crypt foci. One-month pilot, registry UMIN000001241 identified. Crypt-foci counts and epithelial proliferation. Not colorectal cancer incidence. Small preliminary foci changes motivated further research. Controlled change magnitude and long-term cancer relevance remain unknown. Larger randomized between-group clinical-outcome evidence required. The 2016 lesion trial adds evidence but still does not prove reduced cancer mortality.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Nondiabetic adults with endoscopically identified crypt foci. Yokohama City University; major hepatic/renal disease, pregnancy, CRC and NSAIDs excluded. 1342 screened, 629 with foci, 26 randomized: 12 metformin/14 untreated; 9/14 analyzed. Very selected and predominantly male sample. Metformin, formulation/product not specified in the inspected pages. Oral 250 mg/day for one month. Prior screening/polypectomy when needed. One month. Not a recommended chemoprevention schedule. No treatment, not placebo. Participants assigned to two groups. Randomization stated; sequence/concealment not described. Endoscopic and laboratory assessments masked; participants not placebo-blinded. Baseline and one-month comparison. Lack of placebo and allocation detail increase uncertainty. Three of twelve metformin participants lacked endpoint: one stopped early, two refused colonoscopy. All missing endpoints in the metformin arm. Pill adherence not quantified. Complete-case exclusion of three metformin participants. 23 evaluable participants. Participant, not crypt count or microscopic field. Biopsy fields are technical observations.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Crypt-foci count; PCNA proliferation and TUNEL apoptosis. Magnifying colonoscopy with methylene blue; two masked observers; biopsies. Baseline to one month. Surrogate lesion and cellular markers. No established cancer-risk reduction threshold. No cancer endpoint. Metformin foci 8.78±6.45 to 5.11±4.99; control 7.23±6.65 to 7.56±6.75. Nine metformin and fourteen control analyzed. Mean±SD foci per participant. Metformin within-arm P=.007; control within-arm P=.609. No reported between-group change estimate with CI. Significant in one arm and nonsignificant in another does not establish a significant treatment interaction. Early human mechanistic pilot. Indirect rationale, not clinical prevention proof. Authors infer promise; guide emphasizes within-group analysis and surrogate endpoint. Never cite as a positive cancer-prevention trial.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Brief safety narrative without detailed surveillance methods. Twelve assigned, nine evaluable metformin participants; safety denominator not explicit. No side effects reported, including diarrhea, hypoglycemia or lactic acidosis. One early treatment stop; cause not stated. One month. Cannot infer long-term or rare-event safety. Tiny sample, one-arm missingness, no placebo and within-arm testing. Randomization not described sufficiently to exclude selection bias. Registry history and supplementary Figure S1 not recovered. Several foci categories and laboratory tests. No between-group CI; substantial uncertainty. Control age SD printed 90.7 years, evidently discordant with the scale; not silently repaired. No causal effect size calculated from these data. Selected nondiabetic adults with crypt foci. 250 mg daily for one month. Preliminary surrogate signal only. Does not establish prevention of adenomas or cancer, or effect in average-risk adults. Later adenoma trial is a different study and endpoint.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: Hosono 2010 human pilot, UMIN000001241. Related animal studies and Higurashi 2016 adenoma trial. Distinct from animal experiments in the same research program. Current inventory reconciliation. Do not mistake the adjacent leptin paper in the archive for this study. Kunihiro Hosono, Hiroki Endo, Hirokazu Takahashi and colleagues; Atsushi Nakajima corresponding. Yokohama City University and National Cancer Center Japan. Japanese ministry, biomedical innovation, Yokohama foundation and JST grants. Metformin supplier not stated in inspected pages. No potential conflicts disclosed. Funding/COI located on p1082, not the unrelated preceding article. Cancer Prevention Research 2010;3:1077–1083, DOI 10.1158/1940-6207.CAPR-10-0186. Relevant pp1077–1082 visually read in mixed grant archive. Final reference page1083 and supplementary Figure S1 absent. UMIN000001241 stated, separate record not audited. No correction/retraction identified in retrieved records. November 4, 2026. Readable images used because embedded text extraction was empty.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Assess metformin’s effect on SARS-CoV-2 nasal RNA load. Prespecified secondary virologic endpoint, baseline-adjusted follow-up viral load. Biological antiviral signal. Clinical efficacy requires its own outcomes. Metformin lowered average nasal RNA load in this substudy. Infectious-virus effects, transmission and mediation are unresolved. Independent virology with culture plus clinical outcomes could clarify relevance. Rebound reduction remains uncertain.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: COVID-OUT adults with acute infection, overweight or obesity. Optional self-collected nasal-swab substudy. 999 of 1323 mITT participants: 504 metformin and 495 placebo; 945 day-1, 871 day-5 and 775 day-10 samples. Optional participation is a selection step. Immediate-release metformin. 500 mg day 1, 500 mg twice daily days 2–5, 500/1000 mg days 6–14. Factorial co-medication assignments adjusted in analysis. Swabs days 1, 5 and 10. Exact regimen is a description, not a recommendation. Concurrent placebo assignments in COVID-OUT. Parent factorial randomization. Randomized treatment, not randomized swab participation. Participants, care providers, investigators and outcome assessors blinded. Enrollment December 2020–January 2022. Not an independent second randomized trial. Day-10 sample availability lower than baseline. 78 lacked materials for all days and three for follow-up due to supply shortages; multiple imputation used. Drug adherence inherited from parent, not separately established by swabs. Optional sample providers define substudy; nonproviders excluded from its cohort. Tobit model for left censoring, clustered SEs for repeated observations. Participant, with repeated nasal specimens. Imputation assumptions and self-collection variability matter.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Secondary log viral load; detectability and rebound additional measures. RT-qPCR N1/N2 targets calibrated to digital PCR. Days 5 and 10 adjusted for baseline. RNA surrogate; not viral culture, transmission or symptoms. No validated RNA-change threshold for clinical benefit established here. RNA copies do not directly measure infectiousness. Average viral load declined in both groups; adjusted reduction greater with metformin. 504/495 substudy participants; repeated swabs are not additional patients. Between-group difference −.56 log10 copies/mL, CI −1.05 to −.06, P=.027. Day 5 −.47, CI −.93 to −.014; day 10 −.64, CI −1.42 to .13. Detectability OR .72, CI .55–.94; rebound 3.28% versus 5.95%, OR .68, CI .36–1.29. The rebound interval includes no effect; the stronger plain-language summary overstates that certainty. Antiviral rationale. Supports an RNA-load reduction; indirect for clinical prevention. Authors’ mechanistic explanation is plausible but not proven mediation. Do not count as independent replication of long-term benefit.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: No distinct safety surveillance described for viral analysis. Parent mITT safety population, not just 999 swab providers. Parent reports no medication-related serious event. Parent discontinuations, not new independent counts. Fourteen-day treatment; parent serious-event follow-up through day 28. This paper cannot establish long-term safety. Optional sampling, missing swabs and lower-limit censoring. Treatment randomized; sample availability and collection quality may bias substudy. SAP recovered with parent; targeted endpoint alignment, not full reanalysis. Multiple outcomes, drugs, timepoints and subgroups. Day-10 and rebound intervals cross no effect. Summary says one-third lower rebound risk despite imprecise OR; avoid definitive wording. No head-to-head comparison with other antivirals. Early acute COVID-19 in selected adults. IR course as tested. Supports a nasal-RNA signal only. Does not prove lower contagion, long-COVID treatment or superiority to other drugs. Cross-trial viral-load rankings are not valid comparative efficacy.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: COVID-OUT. Acute and long-term companion reports. Same randomized cohort subset. Current trial-family reconciliation. One family, three reports. Carolyn Bramante, Kenneth Beckman and colleagues. US multicenter COVID-OUT group. Same foundation funding; authors state funders had no role. Other factorial drug donations listed; metformin supply not independently characterized. Named consulting, grant, stock and advisory disclosures include Buse, Puskarich, Karger, Cohen and Bramante. Documented without imputing misconduct. Clinical Infectious Diseases 2024, DOI 10.1093/cid/ciae159. Full article acquired. Virology-specific supplementary tables/figures not separately recovered in this assessment. NCT04510194 and parent protocol/SAP available. No virology correction identified in retrieved records. November 3–4, 2026. Main effect and its uncertainty directly inspected.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test whether metformin augments response to resistance training. Registry primary outcome is type II fiber area change; whole-body and thigh measures are separate outcomes. Hypertrophy and strength in older adults. Do not label every mass endpoint primary. Metformin did not augment resistance-training response in this trial. Long-term functional consequences and responses in other metabolic states remain uncertain. Larger prespecified functional trials with complete adherence and harms could clarify the balance. Exercise remains a cointervention, not an outcome to abandon.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Community-dwelling nondiabetic adults, eligibility age at least 65; median age about 69. Kentucky and Alabama; independently mobile, predominantly White, generally high functioning. 109 randomized: 54 metformin, 55 placebo; 94 completed: 46 and 48. Not a trial restricted to frail adults with sarcopenia. Metformin tablets, 850 mg. One daily for 7 days then 850 mg twice daily, with 2-week wash-in and 14 weeks of training. Supervised progressive resistance training three days weekly in both arms. Sixteen weeks of medication, strength baseline after initial training adaptation. The comparison is exercise plus drug versus exercise plus placebo. Placebo with identical training. Parallel randomized allocation. Permutation details are in Appendix S5, not successfully acquired. Double-blind study. Concurrent treatment during the same training program. No metformin-only or no-training group was included. 15/109 discontinued, including six due to adverse events. Observed-data completer analysis; endpoint samples smaller for CT and biopsies. Detailed pill/exercise adherence in inaccessible Appendix S1. Thirteen participants outside BMI target were randomized; five completed fewer than 37 sessions; selected high-quality biopsies analyzed. Analytic sample 94, not full ITT. Person; bilateral measurements and multiple fibers do not create independent participants. Completer selection and endpoint sampling limit causal interpretation.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Type II fiber area is registered primary; DXA, CT and strength are additional outcomes. Biopsy histology, DXA mass, CT area and dynamometry. Baseline and end of trial; strength change from week 4 to 16. Muscle structure and performance, not disability, falls or survival. No established clinically important threshold for the reported percent mass changes. Different measures of hypertrophy need not agree. DXA total lean mass +0.41% metformin versus +1.95% placebo; thigh mass +0.45% versus +3.90%. DXA 46 versus 48; fiber area 30 per arm; corrected relative-strength analysis 44 per arm. Between-arm P=.003 for total lean mass, P<.001 for thigh mass; type II fiber area +14.5% versus +18.5%, P=.610. Knee extension strength +15.3% versus +23.1%, P=.055; corrected relative strength +14.8% versus +18.9%, P=.30. SDs rather than confidence intervals for many changes; lean-mass SD 2.25% and 2.69%. Mass attenuation is supported; a statistically significant strength loss is not. Exercise adaptation and aging claims. Supports reduced gains in some muscle-mass measures; does not support improved strength. Authors emphasize blunted hypertrophy; editorial wording retains null primary fiber-area and nonsignificant strength findings. No general anti-aging efficacy inference follows.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Adverse events collected; main report compares event occurrence. 109 randomized, with 94 completing; exact exposed safety denominator not separately established. More events with metformin, chi-square 9.82, P=.002. Six adverse-event discontinuations overall; full arm-specific event and withdrawal table unavailable. Sixteen weeks. Safety cannot be summarized as equal between groups. Completer analysis, small mechanistic subsets and baseline sex/strength differences. Randomization helps; percent-change analysis does not remove all selection concerns. Registered primary fiber area result is null despite positive secondary mass findings. Many outcomes and tests without a global multiplicity adjustment. Modest sample; strength uncertainty includes no effect. Corrigendum replaces the relative-strength row and updates Appendix S2. Use corrected relative strength, not the stale original P=.188. Generally healthy independently mobile older adults undertaking training. 1700 mg/day with exercise; not a direct test of intermittent self-dosing or other formulations. Training response, not treatment of established severe sarcopenia. Cannot infer that metformin cancels all benefits of exercise or shortens life. Scope the adverse interaction to the measured adaptations.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: MASTERS, NCT02308228. Corrigendum belongs to this trial; CP018 reviews it. No additional independent RCT is added by the correction or review. Current inventory reconciliation only. Keep MET-PREVENT separate because its population and question differ. R. Grace Walton, Cory Dungan and colleagues. Universities of Kentucky and Alabama at Birmingham. NIA R01AG046920 and NCATS institutional awards. Product donation not established by the inspected main report. Authors report no conflicts. Funding disclosure is separate from scientific validity. Published Aging Cell 2019, DOI 10.1111/acel.13039, with 2020 corrigendum. Full report, actual correction and current registry acquired. Five article appendices not recovered through the attempted PMC URLs; posted registry protocol is available. Current NCT02308228 record confirms primary fiber-area endpoint. Correction changes relative strength: placebo 3.89 to 4.62 kg/kg, metformin 4.60 to 5.23; P=.30. November 3–4, 2026. The historical correction is incorporated, not merely noted.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test efficacy and safety for physical performance in probable sarcopenia with prefrailty/frailty. Primary endpoint specified as adjusted 4-meter walk speed at 4 months. Clinical mobility, not lifespan. The tested group differs markedly from healthy exercise volunteers. No demonstrated mobility benefit, with a substantial tolerability burden. Different doses, titration, populations and durations remain separate questions. Well-powered studies in justified alternative populations with prespecified function and safety outcomes would be needed. Mechanistic anti-aging rationale cannot override this direct trial.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Adults at least 65, mean 80.4 years; 58% women. Two northeast England NHS trusts; walk speed below 0.8 m/s and low strength or slow chair rise; diabetes and eGFR below 45 excluded. 268 expressed interest, 112 assessed, 72 randomized 36 per arm; 71 exposed, 70 with final data. Probable sarcopenia did not require confirmed low muscle mass. Aurobindo immediate-release metformin 500-mg tablets. Oral 500 mg three times daily from initiation, without dose titration, for four months. No standardized training cointervention. Outcomes four months; records followed for 28 days after last visit. Poor tolerability may be regimen- and population-specific. Matching lactose/microcrystalline-cellulose placebo. 1:1 via central web system. Minimization by sex and baseline walk speed with 30% random element. Participants, investigators and assessors masked; identical bottles. Concurrent trial August 2021–September 2022 enrollment. These methods reduce selection and measurement bias. Two metformin participants absent from final follow-up, none placebo. Complete-case ITT; high retention despite medication discontinuation. Median adherence 82% versus 92%; suboptimal adherence more frequent with metformin. 13/34 metformin versus 5/36 placebo discontinued medication but continued follow-up. All randomized for stated ITT; 70 complete cases for primary, 71 exposed for safety. Individual participant, not number of walks or adverse events. Retention and treatment persistence are different measures.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Primary adjusted walk speed; strength, function, body composition, quality of life and daily activities secondary. Fastest of two timed 4-meter walks from standing start. Four months. Clinically relevant physical performance. Trial powered for 0.1 m/s difference using its cited meaningful-change estimate. A measured speed difference is more direct than a molecular aging marker. Final means 0.57 m/s metformin versus 0.58 placebo. 34 versus 36 complete cases. Adjusted difference 0.001 m/s, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.06; P=.96. Between-arm difference; per-protocol 19 versus 28 gave 0.02 m/s, CI −0.05 to 0.10. Primary interval excludes the 0.1 m/s benefit targeted in the design. The trial provides evidence against that size of benefit for this regimen. Sarcopenia, frailty and geroprotection claims. Contradicts improvement in walk speed for the tested population and regimen. Authors conclude poor tolerance and no benefit; editorial conclusion is similarly bounded. Retain hospitalization and discontinuation findings alongside efficacy.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Events at each contact, safety blood tests monthly, records through 28 days after last visit. 35 metformin and 36 placebo exposed. 108 events in 35/35 versus 77 in 33/36; hospital admission 12/35 versus 3/36; diarrhea 19/35 versus 9/36. Medication stopped for adverse event in 10 versus 3, and out-of-range safety bloods in 2 versus 1; one metformin death judged unrelated. Four-month treatment plus stated follow-up. Hospitalization imbalance is important but does not prove each admission was caused by the drug. Strong masking and retention; small trial, low adherence and short duration. Randomization reduces baseline confounding; per-protocol estimates can be selected. Published protocol identified but separate full protocol/SAP and appendix not acquired in this packet. No adjustment for multiple secondary/subgroup tests. Precise enough to exclude targeted primary benefit, not all smaller effects or uncommon harms. Figure 2 shows baseline-speed interaction P=.030 while prose says no significant subgroup differences; retain discrepancy and do not promote the subgroup. Null primary result and tolerability matter more than isolated exploratory findings. Very old, predominantly White adults with substantial functional limitation, without diabetes. 1500 mg/day immediate release without titration. Walking, strength and function; not generalized healthspan. Cannot extend directly to younger adults, diabetes care or gradual titration. Does not justify stopping metformin prescribed for another established indication.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: MET-PREVENT independent RCT. CP018 discusses the planned trial; this is its later completed result. No duplicate participant count via narrative review. Authors searched PubMed through September 2024; this assessment reconciles existing guide sources. Do not present CP018's trial-underway statement as current. Miles Witham, Claire McDonald, Nina Wilson and colleagues. Newcastle/Gateshead NHS and university collaborators. NIHR Newcastle Biomedical Research Centre; philanthropic mechanistic support from Alan Halsall. ModePharma prepared matched bottles; Aurobindo product identified. Witham disclosed Rejuvenate Biomed consulting; Clegg disclosed grants/roles; funder and sponsor oversaw design/conduct, not analysis or publication decision. No blanket no-funder-role or no-conflict statement is appropriate. Published Lancet Healthy Longevity 2025, DOI 10.1016/j.lanhl.2025.100695. Full ten-page report acquired; primary table and subgroup figure visually inspected. Appendix and separate SAP not present; main flow and safety data support the bounded conclusion. ISRCTN29932357 identified; published protocol DOI 10.1136/bmjopen-2022-061823. No correction/retraction identified in retrieved current records; subgroup discrepancy retained. November 3–4, 2026. This does not claim an independent participant-level audit.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test growth inhibition and AMPK/mTOR pathways. No preregistered experimental analysis plan reported. Cell proliferation, cell cycle and xenograft growth. No patient survival question was tested. Laboratory activity is insufficient to recommend metformin for myeloma. Human exposure, efficacy and combination safety unknown. Direct controlled human trials with patient outcomes required. Keep the preclinical label prominent.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Human myeloma cell lines RPMI8226/U266 and NOD/SCID mice. Cell-bank lines; five-week-old immunodeficient mice with subcutaneous xenografts. Twelve mice randomized, six per group; cell experiments in triplicate with repeats. Human-derived cells are not human participants. Sigma metformin dissolved in PBS. Cells 5–80 mM, 24–72 hours; mice oral 250 mg/kg/day for 21 days. AMPK siRNA, Compound C and 3-MA in mechanistic experiments. Serial tumor volume/body weight every three days, terminal tissue at day 21. No direct translation of these doses to a patient. Untreated/PBS controls; scrambled siRNA controls. Two xenograft cohorts; assay-specific cell comparisons. Mice randomly assigned; sequence unspecified. Blinded tumor measurement or analysis not reported. Treatment after tumors reached approximately 0.5 by 0.5 cm. Model is established xenograft growth, not naturally occurring myeloma. Animal flow/attrition not explicitly tabulated. Missing values and exclusion rules not fully described. Daily gavage stated; no measured plasma concentration. Cell-line and assay selection limits scope. Assay-specific cultures and twelve mice. Independent culture or animal, not image field. Triplicates and repeated fields do not create patient counts.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Viability, proliferation, cycle arrest, autophagy, pathway phosphorylation and tumor size. CCK8, EdU, flow cytometry, electron microscopy, western blot and calipers. Hours in cells, three weeks in mice. Laboratory surrogates, no clinical response or survival. No patient-important change threshold. Subcutaneous tumor volume is not a validated surrogate for patient survival here. 48-hour IC50 20.2±1.2 mM RPMI8226 and 17.9±1.1 mM U266. Cell triplicates; xenograft six mice per group. Mean±SD; lower tumor growth reported in Figure 6. G0/G1 arrest and reduced proliferation, not increased apoptosis. Exact tumor-volume contrast/CI not tabulated; no digitized estimate claimed. Qualitative tumor direction is used, not invented bar-chart precision. Antimyeloma mechanisms. Indirect laboratory support only. Growth inhibition observed; clinical promise is authors’ extrapolation. No clinical efficacy claim.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Body weight monitored as a limited toxicity indicator. Six metformin-treated mice. No significant body-weight difference reported. Toxicity-related withdrawals not specified. Twenty-one days. Stable weight is not comprehensive toxicology or proof of human safety. Limited animal n, unclear masking, cell-line dependence and high concentrations. Knockdown plus drug inhibitors provide triangulation but have specificity limitations. No experimental preregistration identified. Many t-tests across doses/timepoints/pathways without a stated global adjustment. No clinical effect estimate or uncertainty. Figure 5 legend duplicates P<.05 for one/two stars; model Figure 6 says triplicate despite six mice per group. Do not overinterpret significance symbols or replicate descriptions. Preclinical myeloma models. Millimolar culture exposure and mouse gavage do not establish achievable human tumor exposure. Rationale for research, not treatment benefit. No evidence here of reduced myeloma mortality or safe combination therapy. Authors’ “approved and safe” language refers to another indication, not this experimental use.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: 2018 myeloma laboratory study. External observational reports are background citations, not its own patient data. Multiple assay panels belong to one experimental program. Current guide inventory only. Do not count background reports without assessment. Yan Wang, Wenbin Xu, Zixun Yan, Weili Zhao, Jianqing Mi, Junmin Li and Hua Yan. Shanghai Jiao Tong University-related animal/laboratory setting. National Natural Science Foundation of China grants 81302038 and 81600155. Commercial Sigma drug and named assay suppliers. Authors declared no competing interests. No inference about validity from funding alone. Published 2018, Journal of Experimental & Clinical Cancer Research. Full XML acquired and inspected. No separate supplementary result used. Animal ethics reported; no human trial registration. No correction/retraction identified in retrieved records. November 3–4, 2026. Not a forensic assessment of blot images.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test metformin added to chemoradiation in stage III NSCLC. Prespecified primary one-year progression-free survival. Cancer control and survival. Not a trial of diabetes management. Routine anticancer addition is not supported by this trial. Other modern regimens remain separate questions. Direct randomized evidence in those regimens would be necessary. Do not infer cancer benefit from glucose lowering.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Adults with unresectable stage IIIA/IIIB NSCLC without diabetes. Zubrod performance status 0–1; 79 institutions in US, Canada and Israel. 170 enrolled, three ineligible excluded; 86 metformin and 81 control analyzed. The eligible ITT population is 167. Oral metformin tablets. Escalated over two weeks to 2000 mg/day during chemoradiation and consolidation chemotherapy. Both groups received 60 Gy radiation, weekly carboplatin/paclitaxel and two consolidation cycles. Median follow-up among survivors 27.7 months. This regimen predates routine consolidation immunotherapy. Same chemoradiation without metformin. Central 1:1 assignment stratified by performance, histology and stage. Zelen permuted-block scheme. Open-label; central imaging reviewer masked to assignment. Concurrent randomized comparison. Masked imaging review reduces but does not eliminate open-label limitations. Radiation received by 74/86 versus 75/81. Time-to-event censoring; not all randomized patients received protocol therapy. 52 patients, 63.4% of the reported adherence denominator, completed the metformin course; only 39% maintained full dose without modification. Three eligibility exclusions after randomization. Eligible ITT for efficacy, treated safety population. Individual patient. Treatment completion and outcome availability must remain distinct.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Primary PFS; secondary overall survival, recurrence and toxicity. RECIST 1.1 progression or death; CTCAE 4.03 toxicity. One-year primary estimate, longer time-to-event follow-up. Clinical cancer endpoints. Design targeted 15-point one-year PFS improvement, 50% to 65%; not a universal MCID. Do not equate response biomarkers with these outcomes. One-year PFS 51.3% metformin versus 60.4% control; OS 80.8% versus 80.2%. Eligible population 86 versus 81; survival percentages are Kaplan-Meier estimates, not simple event fractions. PFS HR 1.15, CI 0.77–1.73; OS HR 1.03, CI 0.64–1.68. Estimated PFS difference −9.1 percentage points, calculated from rounded reported rates. Primary reported P=.24; blinded imaging sensitivity HR 1.09, CI 0.69–1.73. No survival benefit demonstrated; uncertainty does not establish equivalence. Adding metformin to chemoradiation. No demonstrated PFS or OS benefit. Authors' clinical conclusion agrees with observed comparisons; do not convert mechanistic rationale into efficacy. Retain dose-completion limitations.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: CTCAE assessment at follow-up; protocol-related toxicity tabulated. 79 metformin and 75 control. At least one grade 3+ event: 52/79 versus 51/75; grade 5 events one versus four, none deemed potentially treatment-related. Metformin adverse effects were the most common reason for its discontinuation. During treatment and scheduled follow-up. Comparable severe-event rates do not mean no gastrointestinal burden. Open-label, phase II sample and incomplete full-dose exposure; masked imaging a strength. Randomization limits confounding; background care and adherence affect interpretation. Full separately linked protocol and supplementary tables not acquired in this packet. Several secondary comparisons; avoid selecting isolated trends. Wide efficacy intervals; trial designed for a large improvement. Abstract age IQR differs slightly from full-cohort table; no harmonization needed for guide conclusions. No validated subgroup rescue of the null result. Unresectable stage III NSCLC without diabetes. 2000 mg/day with specified carboplatin/paclitaxel regimen. Does not support adding metformin to improve survival. Not all lung cancer stages, molecular therapies or modern immunotherapy combinations were tested. Do not generalize a regimen-specific null to diabetes treatment.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: NRG-LU001 independent trial. ALMERA is a separate Canadian trial with different chemotherapy and duration. No duplicate cohort identified between these named trials. Current guide sources, not exhaustive NSCLC review. Both should be presented without pooling incompatible primary endpoints. Heath Skinner, Chen Hu, Theodoros Tsakiridis and colleagues. NRG Oncology multicenter network. NCI grants; NRG/NCI involved in design, conduct, analysis and publication. Donated-product source not established in inspected text. Several investigators disclosed grants, consulting and other industry relationships. Disclosures are documented, not used as a substitute for appraisal. Published JAMA Oncology 2021, DOI 10.1001/jamaoncol.2021.2318. Full article including tables acquired. Supplement 1 protocol and Supplement 2 not separately recovered. NCT02186847 identified in report; separate registry not audited here. No correction/retraction identified in retrieved records. November 3–4, 2026. Main-report assessment supports the bounded null conclusion.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test neuronal protection and AMPK/autophagy mechanisms. No registered experimental protocol reported. Toxin-induced neuronal injury and cell signaling. Not idiopathic human Parkinson disease. Interesting biological rationale with major model/exposure limits. Human target engagement and durable clinical benefit unknown. Adequate randomized human trials with functional outcomes and safety needed. A mechanism is not a treatment result.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Male C57BL/6 mice and human-derived SH-SY5Y cells. Ten-week-old mice; MPTP plus probenecid toxin model. Behavioral/chemistry n=8 per group, histology n=4, MAO-B n=5; three independent cell experiments. No human participants. Metformin from Pacific Ocean, Tianjin. Mice: 5 mg/mL drinking water from day three for five weeks; cells: 2 mM pretreatment one hour. MPTP 20 mg/kg plus probenecid 250 mg/kg every 3.5 days; cells MPP+ 200 µM for 48 hours. Mouse motor test day 37; cell assays up to 48 hours. Water concentration is not a measured mg/kg intake or human-equivalent dose. Saline, toxin alone, toxin plus metformin and metformin alone. Four mouse groups; cell inhibitor comparisons. Mouse random allocation stated; sequence not described. Stereological assessment blinded; other masking not clearly described. Metformin during toxin exposure, not after longstanding disease. Prevention/co-treatment differs from treating established degeneration. Whole-experiment animal attrition not explicitly tabulated. Missing observations and exclusion criteria not fully documented. Water intake and achieved drug concentration not reported. Different assays use different n. Assay-specific animals or independent culture experiments. Mouse or independent culture; sections/fields are technical observations. Do not count 12 sections per brain as 12 animals.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Motor, dopamine, neuron counts, inflammatory markers and signaling. Rotarod, HPLC, histology, western blot, PCR and cell viability. Five-week mouse course; short cell exposures. Animal function and mechanistic surrogate outcomes. No validated human clinically meaningful threshold. No human symptom or progression endpoint. Toxin rotarod 24.7±8.0 versus toxin-plus-metformin 81.7±11.4, reported as minutes. Eight mice per motor group; four per neuron-count group. Reported 25% higher TH-positive neuron count with metformin versus toxin alone. Dysfunctional mitochondria 19.4% toxin versus 8.5% with metformin, 3.4% untreated cells. Means±SEM and ANOVA/Tukey P values; no clinical effect CI. Do not convert laboratory proportions into patient risk reductions. Autophagy and mitochondrial hypotheses. Indirect support for further research only. Observed toxin-model protection; authors speculate about Parkinson therapy; guide makes no human-efficacy inference. No disease-modifying claim.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: No comprehensive toxicology program. Small mouse groups and cell cultures only. Metformin-only controls and viability assays do not measure human adverse effects. Toxicity-related animal withdrawals not reported. Five weeks maximum in mice. Cannot establish safety for older adults. Small samples, limited masking detail and pharmacologic inhibitor specificity. Randomized toxin model limits some confounding; no clinical disease heterogeneity. No accessible preregistered analysis plan. Numerous correlated molecular endpoints; Tukey within analyses, not global correction. Small n and no clinically transportable intervals. Rotarod unit reported as minutes; implausibility warrants caution, no silent unit change. Compound C/3MA reversal supports a hypothesis but does not prove a uniquely specific human mechanism. sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test adjunctive metformin for cognitive impairment in schizophrenia. Current registry lists MCCB at 12 weeks; paper follows participants for 24 weeks. Cognitive test performance and its relationship to metabolic and brain-connectivity changes. The longer follow-up is not silently treated as the registered primary timepoint. Promising but unconfirmed adjunctive cognitive effect in a selected population. Clinical importance, durability, real-life function and mechanism remain uncertain. Larger placebo-controlled trials with prespecified cognition and functioning outcomes could change this judgment. No independent clinical replication is supplied by CP017.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Clinically stable adults aged 18–65, predominantly young, with schizophrenia. Second Xiangya Hospital, China; illness at most 5 years, at least 10% antipsychotic-associated weight gain; diabetes and major physical illness excluded. 72 randomized, 48 metformin and 24 control; 59 completed 24 weeks, 39 and 20 respectively. The completion population differs from the randomized population. Lilinghengtai metformin tablets. Oral titration from 500 mg evening to 1500 mg/day in three doses by day 5, or maximum tolerated dose. Fixed baseline antipsychotic treatment in both groups. Assessments baseline, 12 and 24 weeks. This is adjunctive treatment, not replacement of antipsychotics. Antipsychotics alone, without placebo. 2:1 assignment. Computer-generated random numbers. Open-label treatment; independent cognitive evaluator blinded. September 2017–April 2021. Participant and clinician expectations may affect performance despite evaluator blinding. 13 of 72 did not complete 24 weeks. Linear mixed models accommodate missing follow-up under assumptions; eight lacked week-24 MRI because of COVID restrictions. Pill returns; reported mean adherence 96.1%, all over 80%. Low baseline cognitive-deficit participants excluded from imaging/correlation analyses; endpoint-specific samples differ. Cognition mixed models; Table 1 metabolic analysis labels 40 and 23, despite 48 and 24 randomized. Participant is the experimental unit; brain voxels and visits are not independent patients. The denominators require endpoint-specific reporting rather than a single trial-wide number.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Cognition primary; metabolic, symptom and imaging analyses additional. Chinese MCCB composite and seven domains; PANSS, depression scale and resting-state fMRI. 12 and 24 weeks. Standardized cognitive test, not direct daily-function or quality-of-life improvement. Post hoc responder threshold at least 5 MCCB points; functional clinical importance was not independently established. A score gain is not proof of better everyday function. Adjusted 24-week composite advantage 3.43 points for metformin. Post hoc responders 28/39 versus 6/20 completers. Composite 95% CI 1.83–5.02 points; responder OR 5.94, CI 1.82–19.40. Between-arm cognitive advantage; domain differences also reported, including processing speed 3.75 and verbal learning 5.71 points. Responder interval is wide; no equivalently verified functional outcome estimate. Do not substitute within-arm metabolic improvement for the between-arm cognitive effect. Schizophrenia cognitive benefit and mechanism. Supports a preliminary cognitive test signal, with important bias and functional-outcome limits. Authors' stronger efficacy language is narrowed editorially; brain changes are associations. Use parent results for clinical estimates and CP017 only for exploratory context.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Treatment-Emergent Symptom Scale at each visit. Safety report explicitly uses 45 metformin recipients for decreased appetite. Decreased appetite 15/45, 33.3%, versus 0% in control; other differences described as nonsignificant. Complete withdrawal reasons and adverse-event Table S9 are not in the acquired main report. 24 weeks. Neither a nonsignificant comparison nor the authors' general safety wording excludes uncommon harms. Open-label small single-center study with attrition and selected imaging subsets. Randomization helps baseline balance; expectations and post-randomization selection remain. Registry 12-week primary versus emphasized 24-week report; full historical protocol comparison unavailable. Numerous domains, correlations and mediation tests; imaging used cluster FWE correction but this does not correct every analysis. Cognitive CI excludes zero, while small responder and imaging subsets remain imprecise. Published denominators differ by cognitive, metabolic and safety analyses; do not harmonize by assumption. Correlational mediation cannot establish a causal biological pathway. Stable early-course schizophrenia with antipsychotic-associated weight gain. Adjunctive oral 1500 mg/day, not all psychiatric populations or doses. Cognition test performance, not symptom remission or independent living. Does not establish benefit in diabetes, older adults, unstable psychosis or long-duration disease. The broad term cognitive enhancer would overstate this evidence.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: One parent randomized cohort. CP017 is the 2025 exploratory TCA/hippocampal analysis of this same cohort. 58 metabolite and 33 imaging participants in CP017 overlap this trial. Current guide references reconciled; no exhaustive replication review. Count one trial, not a parent and a new mechanistic RCT. Tiannan Shao, Jing Huang, Renrong Wu and colleagues. Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University. National Natural Science Foundation of China 81622018 and 82072096. Brand/manufacturer specified; donation not established. Authors declare no competing interests. Funding and disclosed interests do not replace design appraisal. Published Translational Psychiatry 2023 report, DOI 10.1038/s41398-023-02616-x. Full text acquired and assessed. Separate full protocol and supplemental safety/flow tables not successfully acquired. NCT03271866 current record inspected; first posted September 5, 2017, after listed August 28 start. No correction or retraction identified in retrieved article/metadata. November 3–4, 2026. This remains a main-report assessment with explicit supplementary gaps.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test adding metformin to standard care for metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer. Primary overall survival; metastatic and nonmetastatic cohorts analyzed separately under SAP. Survival, progression and metabolic outcomes. This report covers the metastatic cohort only. Metformin improved selected metabolic measures but did not significantly improve overall survival. Effects with current regimens and prospectively confirmed subgroups remain uncertain. Direct trials with modern therapy and clinical outcomes could change the conclusion. Treatment decisions require the cancer team.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Men with metastatic prostate cancer without diabetes. 112 UK/Swiss hospitals; HbA1c below 6.5%, eGFR at least 45, performance status 0–2. 1874 randomized: 936 metformin, 938 standard care; median age 69; 94% newly diagnosed. Separate nonmetastatic participants are not added to this denominator. Oral metformin. 850 mg daily for four to six weeks then twice daily, continued if tolerated. ADT in all; 82% received docetaxel and only 3% an androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor. Median follow-up 60 months by case forms, 69 months including civil registration. Current treatment combinations may differ. Standard care alone. Central telephone allocation 1:1 with balancing factors. Minimization with 20% random component. Open-label. Concurrent randomized enrollment. Mortality is less subjective than symptom reporting, but treatment and adverse-event reporting were unmasked. 42 withdrew follow-up consent, 22 versus 20. Metabolic analyses use available subsets; baseline plus 104-week weight in 583. 897 confirmed metformin starters; 28 stopped within 30 days; median stopping time 39 months. 15 explicitly never started; another 24 assumed started because date missing. ITT efficacy; 921 metformin safety versus 938 control. Individual participant. 26 control participants started metformin; no pill-diary adherence measure.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Primary overall survival; progression and metabolic endpoints secondary. Time-to-event models; laboratory measures and weight. Survival over follow-up; selected metabolic comparisons at 104 weeks. Survival clinical; glucose, lipids and weight intermediate outcomes. No universal patient-important threshold for the metabolic changes. Metabolic improvement does not establish prevention of cardiovascular events. Deaths 453 metformin versus 473 standard care; median survival 67.4 versus 61.8 months. Randomized denominators 936 and 938. Overall survival HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.80–1.03, P=.15. At 104 weeks weight rose 2.00 versus 4.40 kg; adjusted contrast −2.48 kg in 583 participants. Weight contrast CI −3.55 to −1.41 kg; high-volume survival HR .79 but volume interaction P=.12. The high-volume subgroup does not establish a survival benefit confined to that subgroup. Survival versus metabolic outcomes. Supports less weight gain; does not establish overall survival benefit. Observed metabolic results and authors’ subgroup hypotheses are presented separately. No favorable subgroup headline.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Routine adverse-event and serious-event reporting; CTCAE grading. 921 metformin versus 938 standard care. Grade 3+ events 523/921 versus 487/938; any diarrhea 600 versus 350; grade 3 diarrhea 46 versus 29. 134 of 510 who stopped metformin cited excessive toxicity. Serious events collected to progression in control and until progression plus at least 30 days after stopping in metformin. Different observation windows and prolonged exposure affect harm comparisons. Open-label design, missing metabolic measurements and treatment crossover. Randomization supports overall contrast; availability-selected metabolic subsets may differ. SAP version 4.0 dated March 19, 2024 inspected for primary and subgroup rules. Many secondary/subgroup comparisons; high-volume PFS interaction is exploratory. Overall survival interval includes no effect and modest benefit. Appendix contents call protocol v21 but embedded protocol is v23 dated October 5, 2021. The appendix naming discrepancy is retained; it is not evidence of a different result. Metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer without diabetes. Long-term oral metformin with predominantly ADT plus docetaxel. No overall survival benefit demonstrated; less weight gain observed. Very few received contemporary AR-pathway inhibitors; no direct generalization to every regimen. Not evidence to replace established cancer treatment.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: STAMPEDE metformin comparison, arm K. Other platform arms and nonmetastatic cohort are separate comparisons. Shared platform does not make all publications independent metformin trials. Current guide inventory, not exhaustive prostate-cancer synthesis. Count this randomized comparison once. Silke Gillessen and STAMPEDE collaborators. MRC Clinical Trials Unit and participating UK/Swiss centers; UCL sponsor. Cancer Research UK, Prostate Cancer UK and UKRI/MRC; funder approved design/amendments, not analysis. Product supply not confirmed in this targeted assessment. Numerous disclosed investigator industry relationships; no inference of invalidity from funding alone. The primary estimate governs the guide conclusion. Lancet Oncology 2025, DOI 10.1016/S1470-2045(25)00231-1. Full report and appendix acquired. Protocol and SAP included; targeted primary, subgroup and safety sections inspected, not every platform appendix page. NCT00268476 and ISRCTN78818544. No correction/retraction identified in retrieved records. November 3–4, 2026. Do not label the targeted audit a complete audit of all platform documents.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test whether complex I inhibition explains metformin effects on gluconeogenesis. No preregistered protocol reported. Mitochondrial respiration and liver metabolites. Not a trial of repurposed clinical efficacy. Complex I inhibition is one experimentally supported proposed mechanism. Relative contribution in human tissues at ordinary exposure remains a separate question. Human target-engagement and outcome studies needed for clinical claims. No dose recommendation.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: Male Wistar rats, rat H4IIE hepatoma cells and isolated mitochondria/particles. Rats 250–300 g; hepatocytes/liver mitochondria often from fasted animals. Typically three independent preparations; four livers per metabolite group; other assays report separate n. No human participants. Sigma metformin; phenformin comparison. Cells 50/100 µM for 24/60 h; isolated preparations millimolar doses; rats 50/150 mg per rat daily five days. Substrate, ADP and glucagon manipulations; digitonin permeabilization. Minutes/hours in isolated assays, five-day animal exposure. Per-rat doses are not human doses. No-drug/water controls and alternative mitochondrial substrates. Preparation-level paired comparisons where stated. Animal allocation randomization not reported. Blinding not reported. Time- and concentration-dependent comparisons. Mechanistic controls improve specificity but do not establish clinical transportability. Animal attrition not tabulated. Missing experiments and exclusions not fully documented. Oral dosing stated; no direct plasma-exposure measurement for every study group. Isolation changes membrane permeability and may lose accumulated drug. Independent preparations or animals by assay. Biological preparation/animal, not repeated instrument readings. Assay artifacts are discussed by the authors.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Respiration, NADH oxidation, glucose production and metabolite ratios. Oxygen electrode, spectrophotometry and metabolite assays. Assay-dependent timepoints. Biochemical outcomes, not patient outcomes. No human MCID. Calculated free ATP/ADP differs from measured total nucleotide levels. 50 µM metformin inhibited glutamate/malate oxidation by 12.6±4.3% at 24 h and 29.4±7.7% at 60 h. Figure-specific independent preparations; control cell oxidation n=18 glutamate/malate and n=15 succinate. Mean±SEM; succinate oxidation unaffected. Submitochondrial particles required about 79 mM for half inhibition. No clinical CI; paired/unpaired t-tests by experiment. Different membrane preparations require very different exposures. Cellular energy and complex I. Indirect mechanistic support. Observed substrate-specific inhibition; authors infer mitochondrial accumulation and clinical relevance. No repurposing benefit follows automatically.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Visible distress and body weight observed. Small short-duration rat groups. No visible distress or significant mean weight effect reported. Toxicity-related withdrawals not reported. Five days. Not a human safety assessment. Small mechanistic experiments, unclear allocation/masking and isolation artifacts. Substrate controls distinguish respiratory-chain sites; other cellular actions remain possible. No preregistered endpoint hierarchy. Numerous biochemical comparisons. Limited biological n and no human clinical estimate. Free ATP/ADP values are calculated; total ATP was not significantly changed. Do not present calculated energetic changes as directly measured human effects. Rat liver/cell biology. Some cell exposures micromolar, many isolated assays millimolar; human liver accumulation inferred. Supports a complex-I mechanism hypothesis. Does not prove it is the sole mechanism, or demonstrate cancer, infection or longevity benefit. Model/exposure boundaries are central.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: Test whether metformin or fluvoxamine improves fatigue in established long COVID. Adaptive trial with prespecified interim rules; the replacement restores a safety-driven dose amendment and the metformin futility stop omitted from the old report. The metformin comparison concerns treatment of fatigue after illness, not prevention during acute infection. The revised report, not the withdrawn original analysis, is the evidentiary unit. REVIVE does not establish metformin benefit for long COVID fatigue; its corrected finding is inconclusive. Dose-specific effects, tolerance, durability and responses in distinct long COVID phenotypes remain uncertain. An adequately powered, prospectively specified trial with stable dosing, transparent concurrent controls and complete source materials could change the conclusion. The original reporting error is resolved by version-specific handling, not by pretending the remaining evidence is definitive.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: 399 adults in Brazil with new/worsening fatigue attributed to long COVID; 111 metformin, 150 fluvoxamine and 138 placebo. 22 outpatient sites, October 2023-February 2025; eligibility described fatigue 90 days to 24 months after infection and FSS at least 3. Metformin comprises 71 participants at 750 mg twice daily and 40 at 500 mg twice daily; all 111 remained in the intention-to-treat analysis. The two dose cohorts are sequential and not an independently randomized head-to-head dose comparison. Both metformin cohorts received the same extended-release formulation. 750 mg twice daily for the earlier cohort; 500 mg twice daily for later enrollees after the April 2024 amendment; 60-day treatment. Fluvoxamine was a separate randomized arm, not combined metformin treatment. Follow-up through day 90; no participant switched between the two metformin dose cohorts. The dose amendment must not be described as every treated person tapering to a lower dose. Matching placebo, shared within the platform. 1:1:1 allocation to active arms or placebo; eligibility could restrict allocation to metformin. Central web randomization with site stratification and variable blocks. Participants, site staff, investigators and outcome assessors were blinded; tablets and packaging were matched. Metformin stopped September 18, 2024; fluvoxamine continued until its later superiority stop in February 2025. Calendar-time and eligibility comparability of shared controls require attention when reviewing the detailed analysis code. One participant in each metformin cohort was lost after randomization; scheduled attendance was 70/71 and 39/40. Missing data were handled with 20 chained-equation imputations and pooling of posterior draws; placebo/fluvoxamine missed visits were also imputed. Gastrointestinal intolerance caused withdrawals and triggered the dose change; a complete individual adherence distribution is not provided in the main report. All randomized participants reportedly remained in the intention-to-treat analysis; attendance is not the analysis denominator. Intention-to-treat analysis with models adjusted for baseline FSS, site, age and sex. The participant is the unit; repeated FSS items/timepoints and dose analyses are not extra independent trials. Missing-at-random assumptions and the treatment of concurrent controls need verification against the unavailable companion code.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: Primary: change in fatigue severity from baseline to day 60. Day 90 fatigue, quality of life and recovery were secondary. Fatigue Severity Scale: mean of nine 1-7 items; EQ-5D-5L for quality of life. Baseline, treatment to day 60, and follow-up to day 90. Patient-reported symptom and quality-of-life measures, not proof of viral clearance or reversal of underlying disease. The sample-size rationale targeted a 0.45-point FSS reduction; recovery was FSS below 3. A design target is not automatically a validated minimal important difference for every long COVID population. Day-60 FSS treatment effects versus placebo: -0.02 (95% credible interval -0.48 to 0.44) for 750 mg twice daily and -0.04 (-0.63 to 0.54) for 500 mg twice daily. The dose cohorts contain 71 and 40 randomized participants respectively; the shared placebo group contains 138. Effects are FSS-point differences in change versus placebo; negative favors metformin. Day-90 estimates were -0.00 (-0.50 to 0.50) and -0.12 (-0.75 to 0.50). Overall recovery risk ratios were 1.09 (0.83-1.41) at day 60 and 0.96 (0.78-1.17) at day 90; quality-of-life contrasts also crossed no difference. These are Bayesian credible intervals; all metformin dose-specific primary intervals include zero and clinically relevant effects remain possible. The corrected conclusion is inconclusive. The null-centered estimates do not prove absence of benefit, and dose-cohort estimates are exploratory. The guide's established-illness treatment statement must refer to the replacement and its inconclusive metformin result. Contradicts treating the withdrawn result as definitive proof that metformin does not work; also provides no demonstrated metformin benefit. Observed estimates and tolerability findings are separated from the authors' fluvoxamine conclusion and the editorial metformin interpretation. No efficacy statement may use the original report merely because it shares the same trial identity.

sections.title: Limits
sections.paragraph: Physical examination, vital signs and structured adverse-event queries at follow-up; CTCAE version 5 grading and blinded review of serious events. Table 5 uses 111 metformin participants (71 higher dose; 40 lower dose) and 138 placebo participants. Any adverse event: 49/111 (44.1%) metformin versus 49/138 (35.5%) placebo; dose cohorts 32/71 (45.1%) and 17/40 (42.5%). No grade 3/4 metformin events are tabulated. The DSMC reported a 9% gastrointestinal-event withdrawal rate prompting dose reduction; it was followed by a futility stop. 60 days of treatment and surveillance through day 90. The dose change is a consequential tolerability finding despite few severe events. Lower-dose tolerability cannot be proven superior by sequential cohorts. Masking and randomized allocation are strengths; early stopping, dose amendment and original reporting errors require careful scrutiny. Between-dose comparisons are confounded by calendar time and different participants; Table 1 shows differences in vaccination and sites. The original report omitted changes that affected the metformin analysis. The replacement describes them; full protocol/code verification remains incomplete. Multiple outcomes and exploratory dose/subgroup analyses are not confirmatory evidence of responders. The small lower-dose cohort and early stop leave wide intervals around metformin effects. The main report excludes diabetes for metformin but Table 1 lists two lower-dose participants with diabetes; stated infection timing also does not neatly match all Table 1 ranges. These are retained as internal questions. The replacement fixes a major historical error without removing every remaining methodological uncertainty. Adults with established long COVID fatigue treated in Brazilian outpatient settings. Extended-release metformin over 60 days; not equivalent evidence for the short immediate-release course in COVID-OUT. Fatigue and quality-of-life treatment, distinct from a new long COVID diagnosis after acute treatment. Other symptoms, longer follow-up, mechanistic effects and generalization to excluded populations remain uncertain. The guide must explain the prevention-versus-treatment distinction before comparing trial directions.

sections.title: Sources
sections.paragraph: S-REVIVE-2026 / NCT06128967. Original P-REVIVE-2026 DOI ANNALS-25-03959; notice ANNALS-26-03050; replacement ANNALS-26-02144. One trial with a withdrawn report and a corrected replacement, not an additional independent trial. Checked publisher notice, replacement and current guide inventory on November 3-4, 2026; no exhaustive new systematic search claimed. Keep the original identifiable for transparency while excluding its superseded efficacy analysis. Gilmar Reis and the REVIVE Investigators, with Brazilian, Canadian, US and other collaborating institutions. Multicenter Brazilian outpatient trial. Latona Foundation funded the trial. Specific manufacturer/supplier details are not established from the main text inspected. Individual disclosure forms linked by the article have not been obtained; absence of conflicts is not assumed. The named funding source is recorded without treating it as a validity score. October 6, 2026 republication, DOI 10.7326/ANNALS-26-02144; not the March original. Complete publisher HTML and formal notice text were saved through normal browser access. Protocol recovered from the registry and key sections 2.1, 3.3.2 and 12 inspected; journal supplement, analysis code and separate final SAP remain unavailable. The English protocol has inconsistencies: section 2.1 identifies day 60 and a 1-point effect, section 12.5 says day 90, and power calculations use 0.45 points. Do not claim complete prespecification concordance. NCT06128967 current registry and posted English translation inspected. Cover identifies original amendment April 11, 2024, ethics approval April 14, 2024 and English translation April 7, 2026. Registration first posted November 13, 2023, after October 18 enrollment start. Protocol section 3.3.2 confirms dose reduction following 9% mild-event dropout. The formal notice says the dose reduction and futility stop occurred in the trial but were omitted from analysis/reporting; metformin is now inconclusive and fluvoxamine results are reported unaffected. Publisher inspection November 3, 2026; assessment November 4, 2026. Original quarantine is resolved to permanent exclusion of its superseded analysis. The replacement has a separate source-limited assessment, not inherited quarantine or invented approval.

The original report omitted changes that affected the metformin analysis. The replacement describes them; full protocol/code verification remains incomplete. Multiple outcomes and exploratory dose/subgroup analyses are not confirmatory evidence of responders. The small lower-dose cohort and early stop leave wide intervals around metformin effects. The main report excludes diabetes for metformin but Table 1 lists two lower-dose participants with diabetes; stated infection timing also does not neatly match all Table 1 ranges. These are retained as internal questions. The replacement fixes a major historical error without removing every remaining methodological uncertainty.

questionAnswers.question: Does this apply to the reader or product?
questionAnswers.answer: Adults with established long COVID fatigue treated in Brazilian outpatient settings. Extended-release metformin over 60 days; not equivalent evidence for the short immediate-release course in COVID-OUT. Fatigue and quality-of-life treatment, distinct from a new long COVID diagnosis after acute treatment. Other symptoms, longer follow-up, mechanistic effects and generalization to excluded populations remain uncertain. The guide must explain the prevention-versus-treatment distinction before comparing trial directions.

questionAnswers.question: Is this independent evidence?
questionAnswers.answer: S-REVIVE-2026 / NCT06128967. Original P-REVIVE-2026 DOI ANNALS-25-03959; notice ANNALS-26-03050; replacement ANNALS-26-02144. One trial with a withdrawn report and a corrected replacement, not an additional independent trial. Checked publisher notice, replacement and current guide inventory on November 3-4, 2026; no exhaustive new systematic search claimed. Keep the original identifiable for transparency while excluding its superseded efficacy analysis.

questionAnswers.question: Who conducted and supported it?
questionAnswers.answer: Gilmar Reis and the REVIVE Investigators, with Brazilian, Canadian, US and other collaborating institutions. Multicenter Brazilian outpatient trial. Latona Foundation funded the trial. Specific manufacturer/supplier details are not established from the main text inspected. Individual disclosure forms linked by the article have not been obtained; absence of conflicts is not assumed. The named funding source is recorded without treating it as a validity score.

questionAnswers.question: Is the source current and intact?
questionAnswers.answer: October 6, 2026 republication, DOI 10.7326/ANNALS-26-02144; not the March original. Complete publisher HTML and formal notice text were saved through normal browser access. Protocol recovered from the registry and key sections 2.1, 3.3.2 and 12 inspected; journal supplement, analysis code and separate final SAP remain unavailable. The English protocol has inconsistencies: section 2.1 identifies day 60 and a 1-point effect, section 12.5 says day 90, and power calculations use 0.45 points. Do not claim complete prespecification concordance. NCT06128967 current registry and posted English translation inspected. Cover identifies original amendment April 11, 2024, ethics approval April 14, 2024 and English translation April 7, 2026. Registration first posted November 13, 2023, after October 18 enrollment start. Protocol section 3.3.2 confirms dose reduction following 9% mild-event dropout. The formal notice says the dose reduction and futility stop occurred in the trial but were omitted from analysis/reporting; metformin is now inconclusive and fluvoxamine results are reported unaffected. Publisher inspection November 3, 2026; assessment November 4, 2026. Original quarantine is resolved to permanent exclusion of its superseded analysis. The replacement has a separate source-limited assessment, not inherited quarantine or invented approval.

questionAnswers.question: Which claims does it support or contradict?
questionAnswers.answer: The guide's established-illness treatment statement must refer to the replacement and its inconclusive metformin result. Contradicts treating the withdrawn result as definitive proof that metformin does not work; also provides no demonstrated metformin benefit. Observed estimates and tolerability findings are separated from the authors' fluvoxamine conclusion and the editorial metformin interpretation. No efficacy statement may use the original report merely because it shares the same trial identity.

questionAnswers.question: What should this change in our understanding?
questionAnswers.answer: REVIVE does not establish metformin benefit for long COVID fatigue; its corrected finding is inconclusive. Dose-specific effects, tolerance, durability and responses in distinct long COVID phenotypes remain uncertain. An adequately powered, prospectively specified trial with stable dosing, transparent concurrent controls and complete source materials could change the conclusion. The original reporting error is resolved by version-specific handling, not by pretending the remaining evidence is definitive.
